items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning in Medical Robotics
items.abstract: The use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) together with medical robotics is reshaping the medical field by the production of systems that are more intelligent, adaptable and patient-centric. This chapter focuses on the essential concepts, scientific breakthroughs and clinical applications of AI and ML in medical robotics. The primary topics cover robotic-assisted surgery, diagnostic automation, rehabilitation systems and intelligent patient monitoring. AI and ML empower healthcare interventions with robotic systems accuracy, independence and customization through real-time data analysis, pattern recognition and adaptive decision-making. This chapter also addresses the ethical issues, data privacy concerns and regulatory frameworks that accompany these innovations. By presenting a comprehensive review of the current capabilities and challenges, this chapter aims to be a source of valuable insight for the researchers, clinicians and developers working at the intersection of robotics, artificial intelligence and healthcare.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Precision Periodontics: From Automated Bone Loss Detection to Patient Specific Care
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is expanding periodontal care from isolated image interpretation toward integrated, patient specific decision support. Current applications include automated detection and quantification of alveolar bone loss, periodontitis classification, prediction of treatment response, assistance with treatment planning, remote behavioural monitoring and measurement of peri implant bone changes. The field has advanced rapidly, and 2025-2026 studies increasingly examine multimodal models that combine radiographs, intraoral scans and clinical records. Nevertheless, most evidence remains retrospective, single-centre and dependent on heterogeneous definitions and reference standards. High accuracy in a selected dataset does not establish clinical readiness, generalizability or benefit to patients. This narrative review explains the principal AI methods used in periodontics, evaluates their roles across diagnosis, prognosis, therapy and supportive care, and proposes a practical pathway for responsible implementation. The most defensible current use of AI is augmentation: standardizing repetitive measurements, organizing complex information, displaying uncertainty and supporting communication while the periodontist retains responsibility for examination, diagnosis and shared decision-making. Future progress requires representative multicentre datasets, external and prospective validation, calibrated predictions, transparent reporting, privacy protection, subgroup evaluation, interoperable records and evidence that AI-assisted workflows improve periodontal outcomes without widening inequality. When governed appropriately, AI may become an important component of precision periodontics, but it should complement rather than replace clinical expertise.

items.title: Artificial intelligence and research integrity in reproductive medicine: reproducibility, transparency, accountability, and responsible translation
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being investigated across reproductive medicine, including semen analysis, sperm detection and selection, oocyte and embryo assessment, prediction of assisted reproductive technology outcomes, clinical decision support, and integration of multi-omics data. Large language models and generative AI are also emerging as tools for scientific writing, education, documentation, and research support. This review critically examines the current applications, clinical readiness, and research-integrity implications of AI in reproductive medicine. Although many models demonstrate promising performance in classification, ranking, or outcome prediction, the available evidence remains predominantly retrospective, task-specific, and derived from single-center or internally validated datasets. High technical performance does not necessarily translate into improved cumulative live birth, patient safety, cost-effectiveness, workflow efficiency, or equitable clinical outcomes. Important barriers include dataset heterogeneity, limited external and prospective validation, inadequate calibration assessment, data leakage, algorithmic bias, limited interpretability, privacy and cybersecurity risks, and vulnerability to performance drift. Generative AI introduces additional concerns, including fabricated references, inaccurate scientific summaries, undisclosed contributions, confidentiality breaches, and the generation or alteration of images that may be misrepresented as empirical evidence. Responsible translation therefore requires transparent reporting, independent temporal and geographic validation, subgroup and fairness analyses, prospective clinical-impact evaluation, preservation of data and model provenance, and continuous post-deployment surveillance. Current international guidance further emphasizes that AI systems cannot qualify as authors and that accountable human researchers must verify generated content and disclose material AI use. AI should presently be regarded as an assistive technology that augments, rather than replaces, embryologists, clinicians, and researchers. Future progress will depend on multicenter prospective studies using patient-important outcomes, design-appropriate reporting frameworks, risk-based regulatory oversight, and clearly defined human accountability throughout the AI lifecycle.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Future of Stroke Rehabilitation in Nigeria: Opportunities for Personalized Physical Therapy, Clinical Decision Support, Digital Patient Monitoring, Health Data Utilization, and Improved Continuity of Rehabilitation Care
items.abstract: Background. Stroke is a leading cause of long-term disability, and rehabilitation led by physical therapy is central to recovery. In Nigeria, rehabilitation is limited by few specialized services, uneven geographical distribution of health workers and facilities, and weak follow-up and data systems. These problems affect how progress is assessed, monitored and continued after hospital discharge, and they raise the question of whether artificial intelligence (AI) could help. Objective. To review how AI might support physical therapy and stroke rehabilitation in Nigeria, and to examine the opportunities, limitations, ethical considerations and implementation challenges. Review approach. This is a narrative literature review of existing academic and institutional evidence. It is not a systematic review and involved no original data collection or AI development. International, other African and Nigerian evidence is distinguished throughout. Main findings. International reviews describe AI applications in movement and gait assessment, outcome prediction, exercise monitoring and remote rehabilitation, with promising but uneven evidence. A mapping review found that external validation and explainability were rarely reported (Morone et al., 2025). No Nigerian evaluation of AI-assisted stroke rehabilitation was identified among the literature reviewed. Nigerian evidence relates mainly to rehabilitation access, feasibility of low-technology telerehabilitation and the state of stroke services and data. Barriers include unreliable power and connectivity, cost, workforce training, data quality, privacy and the under-representation of African populations in AI development. Conclusion. AI has potential to support more personalized assessment, monitoring, decision support, use of rehabilitation data and continuity of care. It should augment, not replace, physical therapists. Realistic progress in Nigeria depends on local evidence, infrastructure, training, data quality, privacy protection, affordability, equity and human clinical oversight.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Paradox of Electoral Integrity in Nigeria’s 2023 Presidential Election
items.abstract: Nigeria's 2023 Presidential Election represented the country's most technologically ambitious electoral exercise, with the deployment of the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS) and the INEC Result Viewing Portal (IReV) to enhance voter accreditation, transparency, and public confidence. Yet the election revealed a fundamental contradiction: technologies introduced to strengthen electoral integrity became, in practice, sources of suspicion and contestation. Existing scholarship has largely examined electoral technologies and AI-driven disinformation as separate phenomena, leaving insufficient attention to how their interaction shapes perceptions of electoral integrity. This study addresses that gap by examining the paradoxical relationship between Artificial Intelligence, digital technologies, and electoral integrity in Nigeria, using the 2023 Presidential Election as a case study. Guided by the Cyber-Elections framework and employing a qualitative content analysis, the study analyses official reports, judicial decisions, election observer reports, fact-checking evidence, and relevant academic literature. The findings reveal two interrelated paradoxes. First, the infrastructural paradox demonstrates that although BVAS significantly improved voter accreditation, IReV's failure to upload presidential election results in real time, together with inconsistent official explanations for the failure, weakened public confidence in the results collation process. Second, the informational paradox shows that the same digital platforms that expanded civic participation also enabled AI-generated deepfakes, coordinated disinformation, and misinformation, creating competing narratives among state institutions, political actors, and citizens regarding the credibility of the election. The paper argues that electoral integrity in the digital era depends not only on technological innovation but also on the interaction between infrastructural reliability, institutional transparency, effective communication, political trust, and digital literacy. It concludes with five policy recommendations aimed at strengthening electoral technology, legal and regulatory frameworks, institutional communication, digital literacy, and independent oversight to enhance the credibility of future elections in Nigeria.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Applications in Fruit Production, Harvesting and Postharvest Quality: A Review
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being explored as a tool for improving decision-making across fruit production and postharvest management. However, evidence regarding its applications, reported performance, and practical limitations remains distributed across different fruit crops, sensing technologies, and computational approaches. This review systematically examines the applications of machine learning, deep learning, computer vision, robotics, the Internet of Things (IoT), and remote sensing in fruit science. Relevant publications were identified through searches of [databases used] covering the period from [start year] to [end year], using predefined search terms and eligibility criteria. Of the [number] records identified, [number] studies were included in the final synthesis. The selected literature was categorised into precision orchard management, pest and disease detection, fruit detection and yield estimation, robotic harvesting, non-destructive quality assessment, and postharvest handling. The synthesis compares the reported performance of AI models, their application across fruit crops, the sensing technologies employed, and the principal limitations affecting field implementation. Particular attention is given to quantitative outcomes reported for detection accuracy, prediction performance, harvesting efficiency, resource use, and fruit quality assessment. The review also evaluates challenges associated with dataset availability, model generalization, computational requirements, sensor integration, and deployment under variable orchard conditions. Emerging approaches, including edge AI, multimodal data fusion, explainable AI, and autonomous orchard systems, are discussed in relation to the limitations identified in existing studies. By connecting reported experimental outcomes with implementation constraints, this review identifies evidence-based research priorities for developing reliable and scalable AI applications in fruit production and postharvest management.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence as a Cybersecurity Support Tool for Nontechnical Users
items.abstract: This research examines the effectiveness of artificial intelligence as a cybersecurity support tool for nontechnical users. The study evaluated ChatGPT, Google Gemini, and Claude 3 across five simulated cybersecurity scenarios involving phishing attempts, password reuse, fraudulent online stores, and suspicious security alerts. Using a standardized rubric, the study compared each model's threat recognition, safety recommendations, cybersecurity knowledge, clarity, and reliability. The findings highlight conversational AI's potential to improve cybersecurity awareness while also showing limitations in the accuracy, accessibility, and reliability of AI-generated security advice. The study emphasizes the importance of independent verification and human judgment when using AI to navigate online threats.

items.title: Artificial intelligence as a driver of organizational digitalization: Benefits, conditions and challenges
items.abstract: Abstract This theoretical article examines artificial intelligence in organizational digitalization. It distinguishes digitization, digitalization, and digital transformation, then combines sociotechnical theory with the dynamic capabilities perspective to explain how technology interacts with employees, routines, organizational structures and adaptation. The framework proposes that artificial intelligence supports transformation when aligned with strategy, integrated into processes and complemented by employee expertise, data and responsible governance. It highlights tensions involving discretion, bias, accountability and the fit between standardized systems and local practices. The article contributes propositions for empirical research and argues that AI’s value depends on integrating technical systems with human capabilities and organizational oversight. AI applications can automate repetitive tasks, analyze large amounts of data, personalize services and support decisions. However, their effects depend on data quality, employee skills, leadership commitment and the organizational context. For this reason, the article moves the focus beyond the simple adoption of AI and highlights the organizational capabilities and governance needed to integrate it responsibly. Keywords: artificial intelligence; organizational digitalization; digital transformation; dynamic capabilities; sociotechnical systems; AI adoption; responsible AI governance.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence for Intergenerational Innovation: Knowledge Transfer, Legacy, and Sustainable Futures
items.abstract: The development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) represents one of the most transformative technological advancements of the 21st century. AI is rapidly transforming human societies and their knowledge transfer systems. While AI’s immediate impacts are currently widely monitored and studied on a broad basis, its implications for the intergenerational compound in society remain underexplored. This chapter investigates how AI innovations reshape intergenerational knowledge creation, transfer, and preservation. Drawing on theories of knowledge management, organizational learning, and intergenerational equity, the chapter conceptualizes AI as an agent of innovation and cultural continuity. Case studies on climate change mitigation, sustainable development, and digital legacy highlight the potentials and risks of AI in fostering intergenerational knowledge flows. The analysis underscores both the benefits of AI – such as enhanced cultural transmission, digital legacies, and novel forms of intergenerational literacy – as well as the costs, including sustainability concerns, cultural homogenization, and ethical dilemmas. The research outcomes cover the use of AI for intergenerational transfers. Positive potentials but also potential downfalls of AI in society in regard to the intergenerational compound will be discussed. The chapter concludes with recommendations for responsible governance frameworks that ensure AI-driven intergenerational knowledge transfer remains equitable, sustainable, and inclusive.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in archives: six modes of involvement and an ecosystem of trust — a reading in light of the theoretical-methodological framework of InterPARES
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) does not constitute a single phenomenon in archival practice. It may generate potential records, support archival functions, assist tool development, analyze holdings, become an object of preservation, or mediate access. Treating these different modes of involvement as homogeneous produces imprecise diagnoses and inadequate safeguards. This theoretical-conceptual article proposes a six-mode model: AI-assisted record production, AI tools for archival functions, AI-assisted tool development, AI analysis of archival holdings, AI systems as preservation objects, and AI-mediated access. Each mode is evaluated against common requirements of archival trust — authenticity, reliability, accuracy, and the chain of preservation — and is subject to a cross-cutting governance framework based on paradata, explainable AI, bias mitigation, ethical use, and accountable human oversight. The analysis is guided by the theoretical-methodological framework of InterPARES, particularly InterPARES Trust AI (2021–2026). The article concludes that AI can support archival work only when its use is governed by archival principles, documented procedures, and clearly assigned human and institutional responsibility. The model provides an instrument for analyzing AI initiatives, designing safeguards, and guiding future empirical validation through case studies.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Education: A Review of Learning Analytics, Personalized Tutoring, Generative AI and Academic Integrity
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence now touches most stages of teaching and learning. Learning analytics predicts which students are at risk, knowledge tracing models estimate what each student has mastered, intelligent tutors adapt practice to the learner, and large language models can explain, grade and write. The same tools have created new problems. Generative AI makes it easy to submit text that a student did not write, detection tools are unreliable, and models trained on student data raise questions of privacy and fairness. The problem is that these topics are reviewed in separate literatures: analytics and tutoring surveys rarely discuss academic integrity, and integrity studies rarely discuss the learning models that produce or detect the text. This review brings them into one framework of five layers: learning analytics and prediction, personalization and intelligent tutoring, generative AI in learning, academic integrity, and a cross-cutting layer of privacy, fairness and inclusion. It organizes 42 studies and compares their methods and reported results. Deep knowledge tracing raised the area under the curve from 0.67 to 0.86 over Bayesian knowledge tracing, and intelligent tutoring systems raised test scores by a median of 0.66 standard deviations. A randomized trial found that a carefully designed AI tutor produced learning gains of 0.73 to 1.3 standard deviations over in-class active learning, but a field experiment found that unrestricted GPT-4 access raised practice grades by 48% and then lowered exam grades by 17%. Detection of AI-generated text is weak: tested tools were neither accurate nor reliable, and detectors flagged 61% of essays by non-native English writers as machine-written. Few studies connect personalization with integrity or measure bias across student groups. Future work should design AI tutors with learning safeguards, assess integrity through process rather than detection alone, and evaluate both under privacy protection and across diverse learners.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in higher education (AIHE): implications for personalized learning and institutional practices
items.abstract: Purpose This study addresses the following research question: What are the implications of artificial intelligence (AI) for Personalized Learning and Online Higher Education (OHE)? Design/methodology/approach A qualitative study was conducted using semi-structured interviews including faculty members and higher education administrators. The data were analyzed to identify the adoption factors, challenges, opportunities, and ethical considerations. An Integrative Model of Adopting AI in Online Higher Education (IMAOHE) was developed based on the empirical findings. Findings AI supports personalized learning through adaptive assessment, real-time feedback, learning analytics, and tailored content. The reported challenges include ethical dilemmas, institutional barriers, and the need to preserve teacher autonomy. Research limitations/implications Limited respondents and lack of student perspectives suggest future research with larger, more diverse samples and mixed-methods or longitudinal designs. Practical implications The model guides institutions, educators, and developers to integrate AI ethically and strategically, ensuring meaningful, context-aware learning. Social implications AI can enhance equity, inclusion, and student-centered learning while maintaining human mediation and cultural sensitivity. Originality/value This study provides an empirically grounded model linking AI adoption to pedagogical personalization in OHE, offering actionable insights for ethical and effective AI integration.

items.abstract: This repository contains the supplementary data and materials supporting the systematic review entitled “Artificial Intelligence in Higher Mathematics Education: A Systematic Review and Evidence-Informed Framework for Productive Pedagogical Integration and Human–AI Interaction” by Felix O. Egara and Alfred M. Msomi. The review synthesises empirical research published between January 2021 and September 2026 on the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in higher mathematics education. Searches were conducted in Scopus and the Web of Science Core Collection, and 18 studies meeting the eligibility criteria were included in the review. The repository contains the original database search exports, the merged bibliographic dataset, the PRISMA 2020 reporting checklist, the full search strategies and eligibility criteria, the evidence-to-framework synthesis matrix, and the study characteristics and data-extraction matrix. These materials document the review’s information sources, study selection, data extraction, and evidence synthesis. They are intended to support transparency, methodological reporting, and further scholarly engagement with research on AI-supported mathematics learning in higher education.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in hospital pharmacy and current application, challenges, and future perspectives.
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is emerging as an important technology in modern healthcare and is gradually changing the way hospital pharmacy services are delivered. In hospital pharmacy practice, AI can support pharmacists in activities such as prescription screening, medication error detection, drug interaction checking, adverse drug reaction monitoring, inventory management, antimicrobial stewardship, drug information services, and personalized patient care. By processing large amounts of clinical and pharmaceutical data, AI-based systems can help identify potential medication-related problems more quickly and support pharmacists in making informed decisions. AI can also improve the efficiency of drug procurement, stock forecasting, dispensing, and medication-use processes, thereby reducing workload and improving patient safety. However, the implementation of AI also presents challenges, including data privacy and security, inaccurate or biased outputs, limited transparency of algorithms, integration with existing hospital systems, financial costs, and the need for trained healthcare professionals. Therefore, AI should be considered a supportive technology rather than a replacement for pharmacists. Effective collaboration between AI systems and pharmacy professionals, along with appropriate ethical, legal, and regulatory frameworks, will be essential for its safe and responsible use. This review discusses the current applications, benefits, challenges, ethical and legal considerations, and future potential of AI in hospital pharmacy practice.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Modern Healthcare: Present and Future
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into modern healthcare, supporting diagnostic interpretation, clinical decision-making, workflow optimization, documentation, patient communication, medical education, and outcome prediction. This narrative review examines the current clinical applications and future directions of healthcare AI, with radiology presented as a model specialty because of its standardized workflows, large datasets, and measurable outputs. It discusses the growing roles of generative AI, large language models, multimodal foundation models, patient-facing applications, and AI-assisted medical education, while emphasizing persistent limitations such as hallucinations, bias, limited generalizability, inadequate reporting, and insufficient prospective clinical evidence. Emerging approaches, including digital twins and agentic AI systems, may enable patient-specific simulation, longitudinal monitoring, and multi-step workflow automation; however, their clinical use remains at an early stage. Successful implementation will require external validation, transparent reporting, continuous performance monitoring, institutional governance, and clearly defined human oversight. The future value of AI will therefore depend not on complete autonomy, but on its ability to improve healthcare safely, effectively, equitably, and responsibly within human-supervised clinical systems.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN PHARMACY: APPLICATIONS, OPPORTUNITIES AND CHALLENGES
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping every stage of the medicine life cycle, from the identification of drug targets to the counselling of patients at the pharmacy counter. This review examines how AI technologies, chiefly machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing and generative models, are applied across pharmaceutical science and pharmacy practice, and weighs the opportunities they offer against the challenges that limit their safe adoption. In drug discovery, AI supports target identification, protein structure prediction, virtual screening, de novo molecular design, retrosynthesis, drug repurposing and clinical trial optimisation. In pharmaceutics and manufacturing, it is used to predict formulation behaviour, guide three-dimensional printing of dosage forms and enable real-time process control. In clinical, hospital and community pharmacy, AI-enabled tools assist prescription verification, prevention of adverse drug events, dose individualisation, adherence support, inventory management and patient communication. AI also strengthens pharmacovigilance, regulatory science and pharmacy education. The principal opportunities are shorter development timelines, lower attrition, personalised therapy, safer medication use and more efficient operations. The principal challenges are poor data quality and bias, limited transparency of complex models, privacy, unclear accountability, evolving regulation, validation gaps, fabricated output from language models and the need to prepare the pharmacy workforce. We conclude that AI is best viewed as a decision-support partner that extends, and does not replace, the professional judgement of pharmacists and pharmaceutical scientists, and we outline priorities for responsible implementation. Keywords: Artificial intelligence; Machine learning; Deep learning; Drug discovery; Pharmacy practice; Pharmacovigilance; Personalised medicine; Pharmaceutical manufacturing.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in the Diagnosis and Treatment of ADHD: Opportunities, Evidence, and Challenges
items.abstract: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a common neurodevelopmental condition whose diagnosis still rests on clinical interviews and rating scales, and whose treatment is limited by partial response to medication, side effects, and unequal access to behavioural care. Artificial intelligence (AI), and machine learning (ML) in particular, has been proposed as a way to make diagnosis more objective and treatment more personalised and scalable. This review summarises the current state of that evidence. In diagnosis, ML models trained on neuroimaging, electroencephalography (EEG), and behavioural or sensor data frequently report high accuracy, but results vary widely across datasets, are rarely validated externally, and have not yet produced a tool that clinicians can rely on. In treatment, the strongest evidence concerns a prescription digital therapeutic delivered as a video game-like intervention, whereas computerised cognitive training and neurofeedback show limited effects on blinded measures of ADHD symptoms. Key barriers are non-representative training data, algorithmic bias, privacy, weak regulatory and reporting standards, and the risk that predictive accuracy is mistaken for clinical utility. We conclude that AI is best positioned as decision support within a clinician-led, hybrid model of care, and we outline the research needed to move from promising prototypes to validated practice.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in the Pharmaceutical Industry: Transformative Applications, Challenges, and Future Perspectives
items.abstract: The pharmaceutical sector is dealing with a number of issues, such as growing R&D expenses, protracted drug development schedules, complicated regulations, supply chain interruptions, and heightened rivalry in the market. The development of new drugs is very resource intensive and often requires years of effort and billions of dollars as well as a high rate of clinical trial failures. The stringent regulatory requirements that demand extensive data validation and compliance further prolong the market entry process. There are also major issues related to counterfeit drugs and poor supply chain practice that are threats to both the business and the public. Artificial intelligence (AI) is one of the answers that can solve these problems with a change. AI-powered drug discovery cuts down on the time and expense involved with conventional methods by speeding up the identification of possible molecules. Machine learning algorithms can also help inform clinical trial designs and improve rates of successful trials by selecting the right patient population and predicting outcomes. AI-powered automation enhances compliance with regulations and ensures all documents are accurate and up to standard. AI can also help to predict demand, detect irregularities, and optimize logistics, minimizing the risk of shortages and counterfeit goods in manufacturing and supply chain management. Additionally, AI-powered personalized medicine reduces side effects and increases therapeutic efficacy by customizing therapies for each patient. Adoption of AI is hampered by issues including data protection, compatibility with existing systems, and governmental approval, despite its potential. With further advancements in AI, however, the pharmaceutical industry could benefit from increased involvement in addressing challenges, leading to improved patient outcomes, more efficient drug development, and better operational efficiency.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Clinical Decision Support Systems for Emergency Department Triage and Acute Care Prioritization: A Systematic Review of Accuracy, Safety, and Implementation Readiness
items.abstract: Background:AI is being increasingly investigated as a clinical decision support tool for ED triage and acute-care prioritization. Machine-learning, deep-learning, natural language processing (NLP) and large language model systems have shown good predictive performance but concerns remain about under-triage, over-triage, generalizability, workflow integration and implementation safety. We systematically reviewed the accuracy, safety and implementation readiness of AI-driven clinical decision-support systems for ED triage.Methods:This review was conducted according to PRISMA 2020 recommendations. PubMed/MEDLINE, PubMed Central, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science and Cochrane Library were searched (citation chaining, reference-list screening and recent systematic reviews were also used). Of the 1076 records identified, 312 duplicates were removed and 764 records screened; 79 full-text reports were assessed and 65 excluded; fourteen studies were included in narrative synthesis. Meta-analysis was not performed because populations, AI architectures, triage systems, reference standards and outcome metrics are highly heterogeneous.Results:Conventional machine learning, gradient boosting, neural networks, deep learning, natural language processing and large language models were included in the studies. AI systems generally outperformed conventional triage for critical illness prediction (hospitalization), intensive-care admission and mortality; reported AUROCs for early mortality were 0.962 and for 30-day mortality 0.925. Direct triage systems also had some success: KATE had 75.7% ESI assignment accuracy; prospective GPT-4 and GPT-4o studieshad κ = 0.899 and multicenter κ = 0.833 with F1 = 0.897 agreement with expert triage but safety outcomes under-triage/over-triage subgroup performance and patient-important outcomes were inconsistently reported.Conclusions:ED triage systems powered by AI have great potential as supervised clinical decision support tools but not yet enough evidence to justify autonomous deployment. Prospective multicenter validation, standardized safety metrics, subgroup analysis, workflow evaluation, governance and post-deployment monitoring are needed before widespread implementation

items.abstract: Description / Abstract Title: Safeguarding Trust in AI-Assisted Credit Scoring in Indian Digital Lending: A Documentary Analysis of the RBI’s 2025 Directions Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and alternative data increasingly inform digital credit decisions, raising critical questions about privacy, fairness, decision transparency, and accountability. In India, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) issued the Digital Lending Directions, 2025 on 8 May 2025. This study examines these Directions as a dated regulatory instrument and assesses their coverage of trust-related safeguards. Reviewing the 2025 framework alongside earlier Indian digital-lending instruments, the study applies a five-part analytical framework developed from the literature: decision transparency, privacy and data minimisation, fairness, human recourse, and model governance. It also compares the Indian framework with international guidance from the European Banking Authority (EBA, 2020), the OECD (2021), and the US NIST (2023). The documentary analysis reveals that while the RBI framework provides robust coverage of lender conduct, data consent, disclosures (such as the Key Facts Statement with all-in APR), and grievance redress, it exhibits notable gaps regarding mandatory pre-deployment fairness testing, ongoing model-drift monitoring, and standardised explanations for AI-assisted adverse decisions. To bridge these gaps, the study proposes a layered set of safeguards: privacy-by-design, standardised reason codes for adverse decisions, accessible routes to human review, and periodic fairness and drift audits.

items.title: Artificial Stone Silicosis: New Face of an Old Disease
items.abstract: Artificial stone (AS) silicosis has emerged as a major global occupational health concern, challenging the perception of silicosis as a disease of the past. Driven by the fabrication of AS products containing high concentrations of crystalline silica (>90%), this rapidly progressive form disproportionately affects younger workers and develops after a much shorter exposure duration (median 7-19 years) than in classic silicosis. As cases continue to emerge worldwide, clinicians and occupational health practitioners are increasingly likely to encounter affected workers in clinical practice. This review provides a clinically focused synthesis of the current evidence on the epidemiology, pathophysiology, clinical manifestations, diagnosis, and management of AS silicosis. Compared with traditional silicosis, the unique physicochemical properties of AS dust may amplify lung toxicity and promote a self-perpetuating inflammatory response. This frequently results in rapid development of progressive massive fibrosis, with disease progression often continuing after exposure cessation. Diagnosis is often delayed because of overlapping clinical features and the limited sensitivity of conventional screening tools, highlighting the importance of early clinical recognition, detailed occupational history-taking, and the use of high-resolution computed tomography where appropriate. Lung transplantation remains the only definitive treatment for advanced disease, underscoring the importance of prevention. Effective prevention requires strong workplace controls, systematic medical surveillance, and appropriate regulatory measures. Clinicians play a key role in early detection, patient education, and mandatory disease reporting. Coordinated action across clinical, occupational, and policy domains is essential to improve recognition, strengthen preventive measures, and avert further cases of this highly preventable occupational disease.

items.title: Ask Before You Answer: A Question-Driven Evidence Reasoning Architecture (QERA) for In-Context Learning
items.abstract: AI assistants are increasingly asked to reason over a user's own web traces: group chats, community threads, activity logs and revision histories. On CL-bench Life, a benchmark of such real-life context learning, frontier LLMs solve fewer than one task in five. We find that the request is not the specification: over 80% of the benchmark's rubrics share less than 60% of their content words with the final request, as for a rule set two turns earlier or every record that meets the user's criterion, and LLMs answering directly pass only 67% of these implicit rubrics against 81% of the others. We propose QERA, a Question-driven Evidence Reasoning Architecture that asks before it answers. QERA first turns the request into a requirement checklist and typed information needs, filtered by code for faithfulness to the user's words; it then answers from the whole conversation, asks the same questions again with quotes verified by code, and applies a guarded local repair. It needs no training or rubrics and makes about four LLM calls per task. On all 405 tasks with four frontier LLMs, QERA attains the highest solving rate on every LLM (21.0% on average, against 18.2% for the strongest of three inference-time baselines and 14.6% for direct answering) and leads every baseline significantly when pooled across LLMs, while using fewer tokens than PSCI and 4-5% of the tokens of Ctx2Skill. Ablations on GPT-6-Luna show that the gain is settled before the answer, by a fixed answer protocol (+3.8 rubric points) and the request-specific questions (+1.6), and that it is concentrated on implicit rubrics, with checking afterwards refining mainly numeric requirements.

items.title: Assessing the Spectral Sufficiency of Wheat Rust Classification: Views and Band Budgets from a UAV Hyperspectral Acquisition
items.abstract: Drone hyperspectral cameras can identify wheat yellow rust but are costly, and labels are scarce. We asked how much spectral information patch-level rust classification needs around grain filling. Using 600 patches of a public ICPR 2026 competition benchmark, we compared the hyperspectral camera’s cube with RGB and five-band multispectral views derived from it, fixing optics, geometry, and timing, and with greedily selected band budgets, under nested cross-validation with Bayesian paired tests and two learners, an automated machine learning search and a tabular foundation model. Five multispectral bands reached a macro-F1 of 0.662 against 0.680 for 101 hyperspectral bands (95 percent credible interval of the difference −0.025 to +0.061, and −0.004 to +0.063 with the foundation model), so neither equivalence nor a relevant gap is excluded, and no greedily selected bands beat them. The distributed RGB images lost 0.117 macro-F1 against the same cube bands, at least as much as omitting the red-edge and near-infrared bands, and an exploratory control traced this loss to their per-image contrast stretch and quantisation. In exploratory analyses within vegetated canopy, the cube kept a Health versus Rust advantage of 0.056 in the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (−0.002 to +0.113), also with canopy greenness balanced, but no wavelength window stood out, and no configuration separated rust from healthy canopy reliably.

items.title: Assistant or Ghostwriter? EAP Instructors’ Views on the Opportunities and Risks of GenAI in L2 Writing
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) systems are able to generate, revise and comment on second language (L2) student writing. However, less is known about where L2 writing teachers locate the opportunities and risks of such systems across the writing process. To that end, this study examined how English for academic purposes (EAP) writing instructors at two universities in Oman position GenAI within the L2 writing process. It focused on, first, the stages at which instructors locate GenAI's opportunities and risks, second, their views on GenAI as a source of feedback, and lastly their preparedness to manage academic integrity in AI-assisted L2 writing. A cross-sectional questionnaire combining Likert-scale items and open-ended prompts was completed by 51 EAP instructors , of whom 49 were retained for analysis. Closed items were analysed with descriptive statistics, Spearman correlations, McNemar tests and Mann–Whitney U tests. Open-ended responses were coded by writing stage through qualitative content analysis. The results showed that L2 writing instructors located GenAI's opportunities mainly in their own preparation of materials and model texts and in feedback. On the other hand, they highlighted its risks in students' drafting and in assessment. Revising and editing was contested, cited equally often as an opportunity and a risk. EAP instructors were more confident in using GenAI to prepare materials than in designing students' use of it at each writing stage. Just over half agreed that AI improves their feedback. This view was related to their overall attitude towards GenAI but not to their confidence as feedback providers. Most instructors felt responsible for checking students' GenAI use and confident in setting boundaries, but their confidence in maintaining academic integrity was unrelated to this sense of responsibility. More EAP instructors reported knowing how to use AI detectors than understanding how such detectors work. The study concludes that EAP instructors' readiness to integrate GenAI into L2 writing teaching and learning is uneven across the L2 writing process. Professional learning and development should therefore target the pedagogical design of student-facing AI use, the evaluation of AI feedback, AI detection literacy, and L2 writing assessment redesign.

items.title: AT-AT: Automatic Tool Optimization from Agent Traces
items.abstract: Efforts to improve LLM-based agents typically focus on modifying the agent itself, yet success also depends on the environment in which an agent acts. Tools mediate this interaction: a tool's description shapes how an agent calls it, and its implementation determines the results and errors the agent receives afterwards. Many tools, such as APIs and MCP servers, are shared by many agents and maintained by providers who cannot change those agents. We introduce AT-AT (Automatic Tool Optimization from Agent Traces), an agentic tool optimizer that improves a shared toolset offline from historical agent executions while holding the agents fixed. A lightweight coding agent reads agent trajectories and their evaluation results, and selectively edits tool descriptions and, when permitted, implementations. On $τ^2$-bench-verified, AT-AT achieves the highest task completion rates in the Airline and Telecom domains at lower cost than strong prompt- and tool-optimizer baselines, and its Telecom gain is statistically significant under paired permutation tests. Optimizing the tools within a coding agent harness also improves held-out performance on TerminalBench-2 and TBLite. When applied to three production MCP servers at a large enterprise, AT-AT lowered cost or tool error rates on every server and increased held-out task passes on one. items.title: Atlas of the Errômetro: An Open GenAI-Built Resource for Learning, Questioning, and Testing Election Polls Against the 2026 Ballot Box in Higher Education
items.abstract: In Brazil's 2026 presidential first round, the ballot box contradicted most polls: 136 of the 161 national polls showed Lula da Silva ahead, but Flávio Bolsonaro finished first. Public debate swung between fraud claims and the margin of error, and no open resource let students verify either with real data. Following a design and development approach, this study used generative AI (GenAI) under human curation to build the Atlas of the Errômetro, an open educational resource in which each section lets users learn, question, and test how registered polls compared with the official result. Data on 1,297 registrations came from the Superior Electoral Court, results were located through documentary search, and automated programs gathered report status and 130 compliance audits. The 901 included polls were compared with the ballot using the declared margin, the A index, the audit category, and a retrospective revealed-efficiency measure. Only 5.9% of the 896 comparable polls fell within their margin (31.5% in the last three days), against about 92% expected under unbiased random sampling; errors were systematic, with 530 nominally significant deviations toward Lula against 82 toward Flávio; Compliant or Caution polls erred less (7.1 versus 8.1 percentage points) but leaned toward Lula as often; and declared cost showed no detectable association with accuracy, with random-sample equivalence of about 2.3%. Each finding became an inquiry users can repeat, with activities, exam-style items, and games verified by automated tests. This first design cycle shows feasibility; effects on learning remain to be evaluated.

items.title: Attack logics, not outputs: Concept-based Property Attacks for Shortcut Elimination in Neural Networks
items.abstract: Deep neural networks (NNs) for computer vision are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, such that minuscule malicious changes to inputs may induce unintuitive outputs. One key approach to verify and mitigate such robustness issues is to falsify expected output behavior, which enables local robustness guarantees and adversarial training. Due to the black-box nature of NNs, current attacks only falsify a class of the final output, such as flipping from $\text{stop_sign}$ to $\neg \text{stop_sign}$. In this work we argue that robustness analysis should focus more generally on logical inconsistencies in concept-level reasoning rather than solely on output misclassification. We formalize this perspective through concept-based properties, i.e., constraints over human-interpretable concepts such as $\text{red} \land \text{octogonal} \implies \text{stop_sign}$ and study the falsification of such properties as a principled form of adversarial attack. Furthermore, an implementation of concept-based properties on already trained NNs is proposed using techniques from concept-based explainable artificial intelligence (C-XAI). For that we formally prove that attacks on concept-based properties are expected to have a reduced search space compared to simple class falsification, whilst arguably be more aligned with intuitive robustness targets. The practical effectiveness of our approach for logically informed adversarial training is shown in an empirical study across multiple models and datasets, including both vision and a security-relevant code processing task. Our results demonstrate that concept-level falsification generalizes classical adversarial attacks: Retraining on our novel attacks maintains robustness gains as compared to classical adversarial retraining whilst better eliminating semantic biases.

items.title: Attitudes and perceptions toward the use of artificial intelligence chatbots for peer review in medical journals: a large-scale, international cross-sectional survey
items.abstract: Abstract Background Artificial intelligence chatbots (AICs) are increasingly being considered for use in scholarly peer review to assist with tasks such as identifying methodological issues, verifying references, and improving language clarity. However, concerns remain regarding their reliability, ethical implications, and transparency. Evidence on how medical journal peer reviewers perceive the role and impact of AICs is limited. This study explored reviewers’ familiarity with AICs, perceived benefits and challenges, ethical concerns, and anticipated future roles in peer review. Methods We conducted a cross-sectional online survey of medical journal peer reviewers. Corresponding author information was extracted from MEDLINE-indexed articles added to PubMed within a six-week period. A total of 72,851 authors were invited via email to participate; those who self-identified as peer reviewers were eligible. The 29-item survey assessed familiarity with AICs and perceptions of their benefits and limitations in peer review. The survey was administered via SurveyMonkey from April 28 to June 16, 2025, with two reminder emails sent during the data collection period. Results Of 66,679 email invitations, a total of 1260 respondents provided survey responses (response rate: 1.9%), of whom 1157 met the eligibility criteria, and 1077 answered the main survey questions. Most participants were familiar with AICs (86.2%) and had used them for general purposes (87.7%), though most report not using AICs for peer review purposes (70.3%). Most respondents reported that their institutions do not provide training on AIC use in peer review (69.5%), although many expressed interest in such training (60.7%). Perceptions of AIC benefits were mixed, while concerns were widely shared, particularly regarding potential algorithmic bias (80.3%) and issues related to trust and user acceptance (73.3%). Conclusions While familiarity with AICs is high among medical journal peer reviewers, their reported use in peer review remains limited. There is clear interest in training and guidance, however, concerns related to ethics, data privacy, and research integrity persist and should be addressed before broader implementation.

items.title: Audit Where Hacks Pay: Budgeted Strong-Verifier Audits Against Reward Hacking in GRPO
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards trains on cheap checks, such as unit tests, that a policy can learn to game, while a stronger check is too expensive to run on every rollout. We study how to spend a limited strong-verifier budget in GRPO, separating which weakly passing rollouts to audit from what reward a caught hack receives. At a fixed policy state with centered advantages, the expected update depends on a design only through each rollout's marginal audit probability and correction; reflecting a caught hack's reward about the failure reward negates the advantages of an all-hack group; and auditing whole groups with the fewest weak passes first (low-pass budgeted audits, LB) minimizes the advantage mass left on hacks among pass-count designs with a fixed correction when a label's value falls with the pass count. We tested this analysis in actual LLM training: from each run's starting state, the sign of this mass on a frozen panel predicted whether hacking would be suppressed in 33 of 39 runs, including 13 of 16 preregistered ones. In LeetCode (Wong et al., 2026) and Countdown-Code (Khalifa et al., 2026), LB drives hacking to near zero, while random audits with the same penalty and budget do not and use more labels. We also find that the randomness of the update affects training: in Countdown-Code, two unbiased corrections, per-item reward-level IPW and a group-level advantage correction, bring hacking down too but end 6.1-11.8 and 8.0-11.5 points lower in held-out accuracy than LB at the same budget. A full audit, which the group-level correction reproduces in expectation, stays within about two points of LB in three seeds, while LB uses 28% of its labels, and allocating the same correction by pass count recovers most of the loss (one seed). Training outcomes thus depend not only on the expected update but also on the randomness of its estimate.

items.title: Automatic Kernel Generation with Large Language Models: Taxonomies, Evaluations, and Cross-Platform Challenges
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently emerged as a promising tool for automatic generation and optimization of high-performance compute kernels. This rapidly growing area spans across hardware platforms and targets programming models such as AscendC, CUDA, and Triton. However, the literature remains fragmented, with substantial variation in generation workflows, training strategies, evaluation protocols, benchmark assumptions, hardware platforms, and reported metrics. This survey provides a structured review of LLM-based automatic kernel generation. We introduce a taxonomy based on the generation-time workflow, separating direct generation, refinement via structured feedback, search-based generation, and adaptive tool-orchestrating agentic systems. We further analyze orthogonal design axes including learning strategy, input representation, output representation, and hardware platform. Beyond method classification, we examine evaluation practices, including benchmark data, harnesses, integrity policies, as well as performance metrics, and discuss why reported results are often difficult to compare. Finally, we use Ascend NPU kernel generation as a cross-platform case study, highlighting challenges introduced by AscendC, host-device co-design, toolchain constraints, and limited public data. We conclude by identifying open problems in robust evaluation, higher-level task optimization, cross-platform transfer, production deployment, and benchmark design.

items.abstract: AbstractThis article explores the concept of Cognitive Surrender in AI-Driven Ergonomics — the risk that as AI becomes more competent in safety, human judgment is outsourced. Drawing on 27 years of EHS experience in Brazil (SP, GO, RJ, MS) managing Safety, Fire Protection and Road Safety in sugar-ethanol plants, soybean processing and construction, and now building EkoSeg EHS US LLC in Salt Lake City, UT, the author argues for AI for Augmentation, not Automation. The study bridges Brazil's NR-17 Ergonomic Work Analysis (AET) and OSHA's MSD prevention, analyzing the emergence of computer vision solutions like Kinebot (Curitiba), validated by Marfrig, P&G, Electrolux, with R$3M investment in Feb 2026 for global expansion. Kinebot delivers 5x faster and 80% cheaper analysis via phone video. The author presents lessons from the 62nd NISO Conference, Killarney, Ireland (2026): dashboards (Power BI integrating Safety Observations, NC, OFI, Near Miss, Training Expiry) don't save lives alone; conversations do. A framework is proposed: (a) Keep the Worker in the Loop — every AI high-risk flag (RULA 7) must trigger a Gemba walk, (b) Use Leading Indicators — % stations analyzed by AI, training validity, (c) Bridge NR-17 and OSHA. Author: Jailton da Silva, EHS Manager, 27 Years in HSE, Founder EkoSeg EHS US LLC & EkoSeg Segurança e Meio Ambiente, Brazil to Utah. items.title: AWARENESS AND PERCEPTION OF ROBO ADVISORY SERVICES AMONG INVESTORS IN MALAPPURAM
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology is changing the financial industry by providing inexpensive, automated, and customized tools to individual and institutional investors, revolutionising the way people make financial decisions. This study intends to evaluate the awareness and perception of robo-advisory services among investors in Malappuram district. Robo-advisors are computer-generated algorithms that provide Investment advice, Portfolio management, and financial planning solutions to customers without requiring much intervention from a human advisor by utilizing Artificial Intelligence and Data Analytics. This study also aims to study the perception of acceptance, its influencing factors, and the perception of investors towards acceptance of robo-advisory services. It was an integrated descriptive research design. Data was obtained from 120 investors made with the help of purposive sampling, using a structured online questionnaire. Data analysis was done using descriptive statistics, weighted mean analysis, and a one-sample test. The results show that the investors had a positive perception towards the use of robo-advisory, and the most preferred domain where robo-advisory services would be used was in Portfolio Management and Financial Planning. The overall mean perception score stood at 3.605 (where '3' is the neutral point) which was significantly more than the neutral point. The perception of investors in Malappuram was found to be favourable, thus indicating the potential for a higher penetration rate of robo-advisory services, also as increasing awareness and information, robust security systems, transparency, and user trust are essential for larger adoption.

items.title: Baby-schema-related cues shape moral expectations about decision-makers: evidence from names, faces, and AI avatars
items.abstract: People routinely form expectations about how others will behave in morally difficult situations, and such expectations guide consequential decisions, including whom to trust, hire, or delegate responsibility to. The present research examined whether baby-schema-related cues systematically bias these moral predictions. Across three experiments with Chinese university students (total N = 858), we tested three manifestations of baby-schema-related cues that share the function of evoking infant-like associations: repeated two-syllable names (Experiment 1), babyfaced appearance (Experiment 2), and visually cute artificial intelligence (AI) avatar designs (Experiment 3). Participants consistently perceived decision-makers displaying baby-schema-related cues as less likely to make utilitarian choices involving direct harm to others. The results show that superficially irrelevant social cues can bias moral expectations about others, although the underlying psychological mechanism remains to be clarified. These findings are relevant to moral psychology, person perception, and the design and evaluation of AI systems.

items.title: Babysitting AI Agents: A User-Centered Taxonomy and Study of Agentic Delegation Failures
items.abstract: Users are increasingly delegating tasks to AI agents, allowing agents to perform long-running, multi-step workflows on their behalf. However, agents may perform these tasks in ways that depart from users' expectations for how they should be carried out, leading to what we call agentic delegation failures. We leverage a large corpus of 163,487 Reddit posts, describing AI agent use, to develop MANDATE: a taxonomy of 23 failure categories organized into seven groups. A follow-up study with 73 AI agent users examined the relationship between prevalence and perceptions of severity and noticeability, finding that failures rated as more severe are considered harder to notice, and that prior experience with a failure is associated with greater noticeability. Finally, we assess the maturity of research on each failure and identify commonly encountered failures that have received little attention (e.g., agents running without making progress). Our findings inform opportunities to make delegation easier for users to oversee and better studied by the research community.

items.title: Balancing Innovation and Humanity: Advanced Practice Nurses Harnessing AI in Mental Health Care
items.abstract: OBJECTIVES: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly changing mental health care through applications in screening, risk prediction, clinical decision support, documentation, and patient engagement. While these technologies improve efficiency and access, they also present ethical, clinical, and equity challenges that must be addressed in advanced practice nursing. This review synthesizes contemporary evidence on AI in mental health care and discusses its implications for advanced practice nurses (APNs), focusing on ethical implementation, equitable care, and policy. METHODS: An evidence-informed review of literature from 2019 to 2025 was conducted across various databases, including PubMed, CINAHL, and Google Scholar. The review covered AI applications, ethical considerations, health equity, and governance to identify themes relevant to APN practice. RESULTS: AI can enhance psychiatric assessments and patient engagement when used as a decision-support tool. However, challenges such as algorithmic bias, inconsistent performance, privacy concerns, and reliance on AI-generated recommendations persist. Emphasizing AI literacy, competency, and governance is crucial for safe, equitable implementation. CONCLUSION: APNs are well-suited to lead the ethical integration of AI in mental health care by merging evidence-based practice and patient advocacy. Ongoing investment in education, policy, and equitable governance is vital for maximizing AI's benefits while maintaining strong therapeutic relationships and quality care.

items.title: Barrier Verification and Leading-Indicator Governance for High-Risk Technical Operations in Oil and Gas and Construction Projects: An Integrative Review
items.abstract: High-risk technical operations in oil and gas facilities and construction projects remain difficult to control because work is temporary, interfaces are fragmented, hazardous energy is frequently introduced or released, and schedule pressure can weaken otherwise mature safety systems. This review examines how safety interventions can be configured so that engineered barriers, work-control verification, competence assurance, contractor governance and leading indicators operate as a connected assurance system rather than as isolated programs. A structured integrative review of peer-reviewed literature published from 2020 to 2025 was undertaken, with emphasis on construction safety, oil and gas safety climate, proactive indicators, digital work controls and sociotechnical risk management. The evidence shows that personal-safety programs are valuable for routine exposure reduction, but they do not by themselves provide credible assurance against low-frequency, high-consequence events. Stronger intervention logic emerges when the control selected is matched to the failure mode: physical barriers for hazardous energy, verified permits and isolations for temporary configuration change, competence controls for judgement-intensive tasks, disclosure mechanisms for weak signals, and governance controls for contractor and schedule interfaces. Leading indicators are most useful when they measure the condition of these controls rather than the volume of safety activity. The review develops an integrated assurance framework and proposes practical indicator families for project and operational settings. The central conclusion is that intervention quality depends less on the number of safety initiatives than on whether each critical control is owned, independently verifiable, time-sensitive and connected to decision authority before exposure escalates.

items.title: Barriers to Adopting AI-Driven Design Technologies in Architectural SMEs in Developing Countries: Evidence from a Delphi Survey in Iraq
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is entering architectural design through generative modelling and data-assisted decision support. In developing countries, most of this work is still carried out by architectural small and medium-sized enterprises with limited resources and uneven digital infrastructure. Existing studies have rarely examined how barriers to AI-driven design are ordered. This paper addresses that gap in Iraq. A literature list of 30 statements was refined by a 15-member Delphi panel into 22 barriers in five dimensions. The measurement model was assessed with partial least squares structural equation modelling on 83 practitioner responses. Interpretive structural modelling and MICMAC analysis then placed the dimensions in hierarchy, and the resulting paths were tested on the same data. Economic and institutional deficiencies occupy the driving level. Technological and data readiness acts as a linking layer, while human and organisational capacity and professional risk appear as dependent outcomes. All four paths were significant, the strongest running from institutional deficiencies to technological readiness. The findings indicate that economic and institutional conditions occupy the driving level in the expert hierarchy, while human capacity and professional risk appear as dependent outcomes. All four adjacent paths implied by that hierarchy were statistically significant in the survey data.

items.title: Becoming the Teacher Poet: Writing Identity, Poetic Practice and the Re-Making of English Pedagogy
items.abstract: This conceptual and practice-oriented article examines the teacher poet as a productive identity position within English education. Drawing on Roz Ivanič’s theory of writing and identity, I argue that teachers’ participation in poetic writing can reshape pedagogical knowledge, classroom relationships and understandings of authorship. I develop the argument through four recursive movements: from writing history to writer identity; from explaining craft to experiencing craft; from evaluator to fellow writer; and from human authorship to AI-mediated authorship. Teacher-poet identity, I suggest, depends neither on publication nor on professional status, but develops through repeated acts of writing, revision, sharing and reflection. The article concludes with eight principles for writer-centred poetry pedagogies that foreground encounter, modelling, invitational sharing, authentic audiences, craft knowledge, relationship and critical human decision-making when generative AI is used, offered as provisional commitments for teachers to adapt.

items.title: Before Blaming the LLM, Diagnose the Workflow: A Role-Level Difficulty Profile for Translating Natural Language into Ontology-Grounded Statements
items.abstract: Natural-language-to-domain-specific-language (NL-to-DSL) semantic parsing systems increasingly translate informal user descriptions into structured artifacts such as Structured Query Language (SQL) queries, Application Programming Interface (API) calls, workflows, formal specifications, and ontology-grounded domain-specific language (DSL) statements. This paper focuses on ontology-grounded Assertion Box (ABox) DSL generation: the translation of natural language domain descriptions into assertion-level DSL statements grounded in a pre-existing ontology vocabulary. In this setting, syntactic validity is often easier to achieve than semantic adequacy. Failures are frequently attributed to weak generator models, but recurring sources of difficulty are also structural: insufficient input, weak domain grounding, output template and vocabulary gaps, weak validation, and non-local repair. We propose a role-level difficulty profile for diagnosing difficulty in ontology-grounded NL-to-DSL semantic parsing at the workflow level. The profile organizes diagnostic variables across five recurring workflow roles: Input, Generator, Output, Validator, and Repairer. The seven variables are input sufficiency, context availability, grounding complexity, template fit, vocabulary coverage, validation strength, and error observability. Practitioners construct the difficulty profile through qualitative judgment over available evidence. This experience-informed, non-exhaustive difficulty profile is intended to support workflow diagnosis and guide redesign or human-in-the-loop intervention.

items.title: Being a role model for preventive action
items.abstract: This article highlights the crucial role of clinicians as role models in fostering preventive action within medical education. Role modeling is a powerful mechanism in workplace learning, contributing both to medical students' professional identity formation and to their self-efficacy through observational (vicarious) learning. Rather than learning from a single exemplary physician, medical students construct a “mosaic” of role models, drawing on diverse professionals who each demonstrate different competencies. This underscores the importance of exposing medical students to varied clinical perspectives. Despite the growing importance of prevention—driven by aging populations, increasing multimorbidity, and health inequities—medical students report limited exposure to role models who explicitly demonstrate preventive care. Preventive actions are often underrepresented or remain implicit in daily clinical practice, partly because curative care is prioritized and population-level activities are less visible. Additionally, clinicians may not recognize or articulate their own preventive efforts as role modeling opportunities. To address this gap, the article introduces a framework describing preventive action at both individual and population levels, structured around three steps: identification, intervention, and evaluation. Building on this, it outlines how clinicians can model preventive care effectively using four phases of role model learning: attention, retention, reproduction, and motivation. Practical strategies include making preventive actions visible, explaining underlying reasoning, creating opportunities for practice, and demonstrating outcomes. The article concludes that deliberate and explicit role modeling of prevention, combined with active student engagement, can strengthen learning and support the integration of preventive care as a core component of medical professionalism.

items.title: Belief-Conditioned Multi-Agent Actor Critic for Decentralized LLM Collaboration
items.abstract: Recent work has explored optimizing LLM collaboration through Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL), but many approaches still rely on predefined workflows, limiting efficiency and scalability. Decentralized LLM collaboration is challenging because agents execute independently with limited communication, share a joint objective, and must infer useful information from communication traces. In this paper, we propose BCMAAC, a Belief-Conditioned Multi-Agent Actor-Critic method that maintains beliefs over contextual information and uses them to facilitate training. Experiments on Minecraft game-playing, web searching and tool-using tasks show that BCMAAC improves task performance and collaborative behavior compared to naive actor-critic baselines. The improvements are particularly pronounced in multi-turn tasks with richer contextual information, where belief modeling provides a clear advantage.

items.title: Benchmarking and fine-tuning large language models for domain-specific materials science: a case study toward GPU application
items.abstract: Despite significant progress in large language models (LLMs) with general reasoning capabilities, their adaptability remains limited in interdisciplinary domains that require specialized expertise, such as those related to cutting-edge chip fabrication in materials science. To address this gap, this study constructs a domain-specific benchmark for graphics processing unit (GPU) materials science, comprising a systematically constructed evaluation dataset and a comprehensive assessment of representative LLMs on domain-specific tasks. As part of this benchmark development, we also develop GPUmatLLM, a specialized domain language model fine-tuned on high-quality data from academic papers, patents, and other relevant sources for GPU materials science. Benchmarking results reveal a notable performance gap among the representative LLMs, with no single model excelling in both general scientific reasoning and GPU material-specific knowledge acquisition. In contrast, GPUmatLLM demonstrates improved comprehensive performance on GPU materials tasks, surpassing baseline models in domain-specific inference while maintaining competitive performance in general scientific reasoning. This work provides an effective framework and practical paradigm for benchmarking and optimizing domain-specific LLMs in specialized materials science fields.

items.title: Beyond "[at]": A Large-Scale Measurement of Email Address Presentation on Computer Science Scholars' Homepages
items.abstract: Publishing an email address makes a scholar reachable, but also exposes it to automated collection. Yet how email addresses are presented on the Web has not been measured systematically across their content, form, and location. We measure it across 32,413 homepage records of computer-science scholars listed in CSRankings with MailScope, which preserves raw and rendered HTML, extracts addresses with a three-stage cascade (rules, then large language models, then a crawling agent), and labels each address. Among 19,517 reachable homepages, we find an address for 17,712 scholars (90.8%). Our measurement yields four main findings. (i) Presentation is diverse: only 53.8% publish plain content, the others spread over 23 subtypes of symbol substitution, code, and semantic description, and 5.5% of scholars' addresses appear only after rendering. (ii) Presentation follows hosts rather than individuals: scholars on one host share a content class in 67.9% of pairs, compared with 38.8% across hosts of one institution, whereas research output and institution rank are barely related to presentation. (iii) Content and form are coupled through code-based links, and 6.2% of scholars with non-plain selected presentations have plain-text copies of the same address elsewhere. (iv) Plain addresses are more common behind passed bot challenges, and 36.1% of redirecting homepages no longer lead to scholars. Human assessment yields 94.4% weighted exact-set agreement on 143 judgeable pages, complemented by three 500-page review rounds with human verification. Presentation is diverse but clusters by shared host, and by our label-based estimate plain-string matching misses nearly half of the addresses.

items.title: Beyond Accommodation: Conceptualizing Disability Health Management for Employees with Disabilities in Malaysian Public Universities
items.abstract: Employees with disabilities may face workplace challenges that go well beyond physical access. These can include difficulties securing reasonable accommodation, risks associated with disclosure, psychosocial strain, inaccessible work systems, occupational health and safety concerns, inconsistent supervisory support, and barriers to career progression. Such challenges can be especially complex in higher education institutions, where academic and non-academic staff work across varied organizational, physical, digital, and professional settings.Although international rights frameworks and Malaysian disability and higher-education policies support disability-inclusive employment, institutional responses may still be fragmented across human resource management, disability support services, occupational safety and health, facilities,information technology, wellness services, and line management. This conceptual paper proposes Disability Health Management as an integrated, rights-based organizational approach to supporting the health, functioning, safety, inclusion, and sustainable work participation of EWD in Malaysian public universities. Drawing on the Social Relational Model of Disability, the World Health Organization’s International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health, and Job Demands–Resources theory, the paper develops a provisional conceptual framework organized around nine interconnected domains: governance and accountability; safe disclosure and confidentiality; reasonable accommodation and assistive technology; accessible physical and digital environments; occupational health, safety and emergency preparedness; psychosocial well-being and anti-ableism; supervisor and workforce capability; career sustainability, retention and progression; and monitoring, evaluation and continuous improvement.In doing so, the framework moves disability management beyond isolated accommodation towards a coordinated university workplace system.It also provides a theoretical foundation for the later empirical development, validation, and implementation testing of a context-specific DHM Model in Malaysian public higher education institutions.
