items.title: Beyond AI detection: traceable assessment design for generative AI-supported professional coursework
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) challenges final-product-only coursework assessment: a polished report or design proposal may no longer show how students used AI, which claims they checked, how they attributed sources and AI contributions, or what they revised. This study examined traceable assessment design as a practical response. Rather than relying on AI detection or broad permission rules, assessment tasks were redesigned to collect evidence of students’ AI use, verification, attribution, feedback-mediated revision, and reflective judgement. Using a multi-cycle action research design with an embedded mixed-methods approach, we studied two professional courses: anatomy and physiology as the main evaluation setting and modern microscopy as a secondary adaptation setting. Data sources included coursework, AI-use statements, verification logs, assessment records, student interviews, teacher redesign logs, and traceability-related process indicators. In the main setting, the redesign class recorded higher cumulative report scores than the comparison class (21.59 vs 17.91/30; mean difference = 3.68, 95% CI [1.80, 5.56], Welch t (63.1) = 3.91, p < 0.001, d = 0.96). Of this difference, 3.29 points (89.4%) were concentrated in the redesign-targeted disclosure/citation, verification, and reflection dimensions, compared with 0.39 points across physiology accuracy and the data/evidence chain. The redesign class also recorded higher scores on a design-aligned ethics-focused assessment (14.53 vs 12.36/20; mean difference = 2.17, 95% CI [1.08, 3.26], Welch t (63.9) = 3.99, p < 0.001, d = 0.98), which was not independent evidence of broader ethical learning. Neither OSPE comparison was statistically significant ( p = 127 and 0.334). Across implementation phases, AI-use statement uptake was 88.2% and 91.2%, and verification-log completeness was 1.44 and 1.74. In microscopy, group report scores across three technically different assignments (7.60, 8.03, and 8.60/10) were interpreted descriptively, not as longitudinal improvement. items.title: Beyond Being Accurate: Implications for Using Natural Language Descriptions for Accessible 3D Modeling with~Blind and Low Vision Makers
items.abstract: People who are blind or have low vision (BLV) are largely excluded from 3D modeling tools that rely on visual representations of geometry. Natural language descriptions offer a potential path to accessibility, but it is unclear whether language alone can support the deep spatial understanding that editing, not just browsing, requires. Advances in generative AI offer the promise of automatic model description, yet descriptions suited to BLV modelers are structurally distinct from alt-text and from existing 3D model captioning datasets, and the domain-specific requirements for generating them are not well understood. We address this through two coordinated studies: an autoethnographic pilot in which the blind first author worked with 12 sighted participants to develop a taxonomy of descriptive strategies, and a Wizard-of-Oz main study that applied those strategies as idealized scripts with 10 BLV participants. We identify a systematic use-to-editing gap: descriptions that support accurate but incomplete mental models are insufficient for specifying modifications, because editing requires knowing the state of features the user did not know to ask about. We show that this gap produces four failure types (accuracy, completeness, expression, and navigation) that accuracy-focused evaluation frameworks cannot detect. We propose a two-phase evaluation framework that diagnoses the failure type a description system exhibits and guides developers toward targeted design interventions, thereby providing a methodological standard for assessing whether description-based systems genuinely support BLV modelers as creators.
topics: Assistive Technology in Communication and Mobility

items.title: Beyond Federated Learning: Decentralized Agentic Systems for Self-Evolving Clinical Intelligence
items.abstract: Clinical expertise is inherently distributed: it resides not in any single dataset or institution but in the accumulated reasoning experiences of thousands of clinicians navigating diverse patient populations, resource constraints, and evolving treatment protocols. Yet current approaches to scaling medical AI, from centralized large language models to federated learning, remain anchored to a data-centric paradigm that treats knowledge as static parameters to be aggregated. In this Perspective, we argue for a fundamental shift from data aggregation to experience aggregation. We propose Decentralized Agentic Systems (DAS), a framework in which distributed AI agents operating across healthcare institutions synthesize collective clinical intelligence by sharing abstracted reasoning trajectories rather than raw data or model parameters. Unlike federated learning, which averages numerical gradients across homogeneous model architectures, DAS exchanges structured records of clinical reasoning, specifically the sequence of observations, hypotheses, tool invocations, and outcome feedback that constitute diagnostic experience. We examine the architectural principles, deployment considerations, governance requirements, and critical open challenges of this framework, laying the groundwork for a collaborative medical AI ecosystem where distributed expertise autonomously adapts to the complexities of longitudinal patient care.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

items.abstract: Demand for mentored undergraduate research, scholarship, and creative inquiry (URSCI) opportunities has grown in tandem with research confirming its benefits. Faculty-driven, hypothesis-testing, discipline-centered URSCI is typical; however, students as partners may also contribute meaningfully to operational enhancement or institutional effectiveness (IE) efforts. Building on a student-staff partnership ideal, we developed a potentially scalable model for student-powered, action-focused URSCI, described here using a reflective case study approach. Student-researchers from multiple majors at a large, public university contributed alongside staff to the Information Technology Division’s generative AI support work through a project assessing how undergraduates experience AI advertising. Here, we focus on the processes and structures entailed and the benefits to student collaborators. We also address areas for future research regarding IE as an emerging arena for partner-based URSCI. The analysis contributes conceptually by broadening the URSCI and thereby the Students-as-Partners framework, revealing how and why IE can and should count as a viable—and meaningful—pedagogical domain.

items.title: Beyond trustworthiness: Psychological and institutional drivers of university students' AI chatbot adoption in Vietnam
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots are increasingly used in higher education, but it remains unclear whether factors associated with perceived trustworthiness are also associated with students' intentions to adopt them. Drawing on an extended UTAUT2 framework, this study examines how chatbot-specific attributes are associated with trustworthiness, performance expectancy, and hedonic motivation, and how these appraisals, together with UTAUT2 factors, relate to behavioral intention. Survey data from 604 university students in Vietnam were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The results show that ethics (β = 0.294, p < .001) and design (β = 0.458, p < .001) were positively associated with perceived trustworthiness, while social influence was not. Design and interactivity were positively associated with performance expectancy and hedonic motivation. However, perceived trustworthiness (β = 0.043, p = .153), hedonic motivation, and effort expectancy were not significantly associated with behavioral intention. Instead, behavioral intention was most strongly associated with price value (β = 0.408, p < .001), performance expectancy (β = 0.281, p < .001), social influence, and facilitating conditions, and was strongly associated with students' self-reported continued-use tendency (β = 0.754, p < .001). Perceived trustworthiness was not independently associated with behavioral intention in the present model, whereas price value and performance expectancy showed the largest positive associations with intention. This pattern highlights the value of considering trustworthiness alongside instrumental, social, and institutional evaluations when explaining AI-chatbot adoption. The study extends UTAUT2 by integrating these adoption evaluations with an assurance-oriented appraisal of the AI system.

items.title: Bias Cues and the Turn to AI: Perspectives from Minority and Marginalized Groups
items.abstract: AI is often criticized for perpetuating social inequality, yet the people most vulnerable to human prejudice may embrace AI as a fairer referee. We tested this paradox across four vignette pre-registered experiments conducted in two social contexts (gender and race), manipulating bias cues (equal vs. unequal) and psychological perspective in the scenario (self vs. third person). When bias was made salient, participants consistently preferred AI to humans. In the gender context, female participants increased AI preference when they imagined themselves as the victim of discrimination, whereas participants with higher perceived marginalization did so when the threat was described in the third person. Such differences between self- and third-person perspectives were not found in the race context. These findings suggest a complex, strategic calculus among vulnerable populations, yet highlight an ethical tension: relying on an ‘impartial’ AI risks masking systemic inequities individuals are attempting to bypass.

items.title: Blockchain-Based Security for IOT and Wireless Sensor Networks: A Critical Review and Roadmap for Lightweight Intrusion Detection
items.abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) and wireless sensor networks (WSNs) rely on large numbers of small devices that have limited energy, memory, and computing power and that are exposed to physical and network attacks. Blockchain and machine learning have been proposed as complementary tools for protecting such systems, but their cost and trust assumptions remain debated. This paper presents a focused review of 35 peer-reviewed studies, 32 of them published between 2022 and 2026, on blockchain-based security for IoT and WSNs. The studies are organised into eight themes: reviews and foundations, WSN intrusion detection, recent integrated frameworks, authentication and access control, consensus and scalability, artificial-intelligence-based trust and detection, privacy and federated learning, and post-quantum security. The paper compares representative frameworks and examines one recent two-layer intrusion detection system in detail, covering its design, threat model, reported results, and limits. The review finds that most solutions are evaluated only in simulations or small prototypes, that many depend on a few trusted nodes, that ledger growth and message overhead are seldom measured, that false alarms and detector cost receive little attention, and that attack coverage is narrow. Seven research gaps and six research directions are derived, and a roadmap for a lightweight, fairly evaluated, blockchain-based intrusion detection framework is outlined. The review is intended to help researchers select design options and evaluation practices for secure IoT systems. Keywords— Blockchain; Internet of Things; wireless sensor networks; intrusion detection; machine learning; lightweight security

items.title: Booked to Disappoint
items.abstract: Three friends, scattered across Brazil and reunited for one long-awaited weekend, booked a glowing, highly rated beach pousada through a leading online travel platform; on arrival, late at night, the place bore almost no resemblance to its listing. Their disappointment is one of millions. Online platforms now dominate how the world books a bed – roughly seven in ten travel bookings are made online, and Booking Holdings alone earned nearly US$24 billion in 2024 – and the reviews and glossy images that once inspired confidence are being eroded by manipulated and AI-written content: in 2024 the review site TripAdvisor removed 2.7 million fake reviews, including 214,000 it judged written by artificial intelligence. Yet the platform is no neutral referee – it earns a commission of 15–25 per cent on the very listings it ranks, while honest small hotels are squeezed and travellers are left to carry the risk. For Maya Fernandes, head of trust and safety at a leading platform, the question is stark: how far should an open marketplace go to guarantee experiences it profits from but does not own? Learning Outcomes After working through this case, students will be able to: Explain the role of online travel agencies in how accommodation is sold, and why online marketplaces both empower and expose travellers. Analyse how reviews work as a signal of trust, and how fake and AI-generated reviews undermine it. Evaluate the conflict of interest created when a platform profits from, and ranks, the listings it is meant to police. Assess the responses of hotels (direct booking), regulators and the industry to the erosion of trust. Recommend strategies to strengthen trust and accountability in digital accommodation marketplaces.

items.title: Breaking the Protocol: Security Analysis of the Model Context Protocol Specification and Prompt Injection Vulnerabilities in Tool-Integrated LLM Agents
items.abstract: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) has emerged as a de facto standard for integrating Large Language Models with external tools, yet no formal security analysis of the protocol specification exists. We present the first rigorous security analysis of MCP's architectural design, identifying three fundamental protocol-level vulnerabilities: (1) absence of capability attestation allowing servers to claim arbitrary permissions, (2) bidirectional sampling without origin authentication enabling server-side prompt injection, and (3) implicit trust propagation in multi-server configurations. We implement MCPBench, a novel framework bridging existing agent security benchmarks to MCP-compliant infrastructure, enabling direct measurement of protocol-specific attack surfaces. Through controlled experiments on 847 attack scenarios across five MCP server implementations, we demonstrate that MCP's architectural choices amplify attack success rates by 23--41% compared to equivalent non-MCP integrations. We propose MCPSec, a backward-compatible protocol extension adding capability attestation and message authentication, reducing attack success rates from 52.8% to 12.4% with median latency overhead of 8.3ms per message. Our findings establish that MCP's security weaknesses are architectural rather than implementation-specific, requiring protocol-level remediation.

items.title: Calculated Logos. Towards an Ontology of Being as Sub-posed
items.abstract: Abstract (English).This note records, in nineteen propositions, the outline of an ontology of calculated logos. Its central thesis is that calculated logos is the essence of beings, to the extent that it advances: to be is calculated logos. The corresponding mode of being is sub-position (supposition): beings are placed under weighing calculation, taken for what calculated logos says of them, and are in force as supposed for as long as the weighting is renewed. Essence and mode of being call for each other, and the logos that says beings is subjected to the same calculation: it is calculated calculation, and the measure passes to the weighting. Large language models are its present hinge; its most advanced field is science and technology. The circle by which what has been actualised is compressed into weights and the weights actualise again also calculates the calculator and tends to close upon itself. items.title: CalibraRL: Confidence-Calibrated Reinforcement Learning for Mitigating Hallucinations in RAG
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often produce plausible but incorrect answers, motivating reinforcement learning methods that reward correct answers, penalize incorrect answers, and allow abstention. However, fixed outcome-based rewards do not distinguish incorrect responses with different confidence levels or account for differences in answering reliability across queries. Consequently, such rewards may inadequately penalize overconfident errors and fail to discourage unnecessary abstention. We propose CalibraRL, a reinforcement learning framework that incorporates response confidence and query-level answering evidence into reward design. For non-abstaining responses, CalibraRL combines correctness-based utility with a Brier-based penalty that encourages agreement between confidence and correctness. For abstentions, it estimates conditional answering reliability using a Beta posterior derived from the correctness of non-abstaining responses within each sampled group. The abstention reward increases with the posterior probability that the model's accuracy on non-abstaining responses is below a predefined threshold. CalibraRL reuses training rollouts without requiring additional annotations indicating whether the model knows the answer to each question. Experiments on three QA datasets demonstrate that CalibraRL improves answer precision and reduces hallucinations compared with strong baselines. Further analysis shows that CalibraRL reduces mean expected calibration error (ECE) by 30.8\% across two backbone models and three datasets, highlighting its potential to improve the reliability of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) in web search.

items.title: Calibrated Generative AI as Meta-Reviewer: A Systemic Functional Linguistics Discourse Analysis of Reviews of Peer Reviews
items.abstract: This study investigates the use of generative AI to support formative assessment through machine-generated reviews of peer reviews (meta-feedback) in graduate online courses in a public university in the United States. Drawing on Systemic Functional Linguistics and Appraisal Theory, we analyzed 120 meta-reviews to explore how generative AI feedback constructs meaning across ideational, interpersonal, and textual dimensions. The findings suggest that generative AI can approximate key rhetorical and relational features of effective human feedback, offering directive clarity while also maintaining a supportive stance. The reviews analyzed demonstrated a balance of praise and constructive critique, alignment with rubric expectations, and structured staging that foregrounded student agency. By modeling these qualities, AI meta-feedback has the potential to scaffold feedback literacy and enhance leaners’ engagement with peer review. We conclude that calibrated AI, when embedded in thoughtfully designed workflows, can contribute to hybrid human–AI feedback ecosystems, while also requiring critical attention to its limitations and contextual adaptation in educational practice.

items.title: Can AI Guide Testing Without Generating Tests? A Comparative Study of AI-Assisted Unit Testing
items.abstract: Recent advances in generative AI have enabled assistants to generate increasingly sophisticated executable unit tests. However, novices may accept these outputs without independently identifying what to test, evaluating test-suite completeness, or verifying correctness, potentially limiting opportunities to develop essential testing skills. Although prior work has explored AI-assisted test generation and feedback-oriented programming tutors, little is known about whether AI can support novices' testing practices without generating tests for them. To investigate this, we introduce TestCompass, a generative AI tutor that provides targeted feedback on weaknesses in students' test suites without generating executable tests. In a classroom study with 18 students, we compared TestCompass with a general AI assistant across two Java unit-testing tasks, examining students' testing behaviors, test-suite quality, and subjective experiences. We found that participants using the general-purpose AI assistant produced more tests, whereas TestCompass participants spent more time developing and verifying tests themselves. However, most test-suite quality measures were comparable between conditions, and TestCompass participants achieved similar requirement coverage with significantly fewer test methods ($p=0.012$) in one task. Neither group reported short-term improvements in perceived testing knowledge or confidence. These findings suggest that feedback-oriented AI can support meaningful testing outcomes while preserving opportunities for hands-on testing practice, offering a complementary approach to AI-assisted testing education.

items.title: Can Open Be Too Open? On the Security and Trustworthiness of Fully Transparent LLMs
items.abstract: There are different levels of transparency for LLMs: open weights, open data, and/or open pipeline. Recently, more interest has emerged in fully transparent LLMs, i.e., LLMs with fully open weights, data, and training pipeline. Drawing analogies to other fields such as software security, it is often believed that increasing transparency inherently increases the security and trustworthiness of the LLM. However, we argue that such claims need to be critically re-evaluated in the context of LLMs. In this paper, we analyze the impact of transparency on LLM security and trustworthiness by reviewing the relevant literature. Our core findings are that, due to the limited reproducibility of LLM pipelines, in practice, users cannot verify the correspondence between open weights and the associated open data and pipeline. Thus, in order to trust a model, users still need to trust that developers acted honestly, reducing the benefits over models that provide less "transparency". Moreover, we find that even when LLMs are fully transparent and trusted, this openness can favor adversaries. Open weights in particular, but also open data and pipelines, can increase the success rate of attacks. Although the same mechanisms can be used to improve the model and protect it against attacks, the current lack of robust lightweight mechanisms to patch LLM vulnerabilities limits the benefits of openness at this time. We note that our analysis is based on current LLM capabilities and analysis tools, and that future developments may require a re-evaluation of these points.

items.title: CANS: Capability-Preserving Neuron Steering for Large Language Models
items.abstract: Activation steering offers training-free and dynamic control of target behaviors in large language models, but existing methods can impair general capabilities and require domain-specific intervention designs. We introduce Capability-Preserving Neuron Steering (CANS), a unified framework that balances target-behavior control with capability preservation. To make target-behavior improvement and general-capability preservation tractable, we introduce two proxies: log-probabilities of target tokens in model generated responses, and output-distribution KL divergence on general-purpose inputs. Combining the local approximation of the two proxies yields a closed-form solution, enabling lightweight steering without iterative model training or additional inference-time computation. The resulting neuron-wise scaling coefficients achieve effective steering while limiting general-capability loss. A shared data-construction and intervention procedure supports adaptation across domains using sampled responses with target-behavior filtering and target-span annotations. Across safety, toxicity, and hallucination control on Qwen and Llama models, CANS achieves comparable or better steering while better preserving MMLU, BBH, and IFEval performance than SFT, CAA, and neuron-level baselines. On Qwen3-4B, CANS reduces HarmBench attack success from $15.50\%$ to $1.75\%$ with a $1.11$-point decrease in average capability. These results support CANS as a practical approach to behavioral control across domains.

items.title: Care Ethics for AI Governance in Higher Education
items.abstract: Higher education institutions have adopted artificial intelligence (AI) tools for proctoring, writing detection, student-success prediction, and student support at a pace that has outrun the ethical frameworks meant to govern them. Institutional AI policy has largely borrowed the fairness, accountability, and transparency vocabulary of commercial AI ethics, supplemented by an academic integrity frame focused on student misuse. Empirical studies document harms these frames are poorly equipped to register: automated proctoring that flags Black students and students with darker skin tones at higher rates, AI-text detectors that misclassify non-native English writing as machine-generated, and student-success models that are less accurate for racially minoritized students. This conceptual article introduces the Jones AI Ethics Framework for institutional use. The framework derives five components (Attentiveness, Responsibility, Competence, Responsiveness, and Trust) from Tronto's phases of care and operationalizes each through a corresponding domain of the Multicultural and Social Justice Counseling Competencies (MSJCC) and is positioned alongside UNESCO's (2021) Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence. The article describes how the framework was developed, specifies its contribution relative to existing care-ethics scholarship on AI, and applies it to two evidence-informed illustrative scenarios: algorithmic proctoring and AI-assisted writing detection. Five recommendations for faculty governance bodies, academic leaders, student affairs professionals, and faculty developers are each mapped to the framework's components. Limitations include the framework's conceptual status, its origin in counselor education, and the need for empirical validation.

items.title: CareGenerative AI in Teacher Education: Capabilities and Biases of Large Language Models in Situational Judgment Tests and Pedagogical Decision-Making
items.abstract: The integration of generative artificial intelligence, particularly Large Language Models (LLMs), into teacher education represents a transformative yet contested development. This article examines the capabilities and biases of LLMs when applied to two critical domains in teacher preparation: situational judgment tests (SJTs) for assessing professional knowledge, and pedagogical decision-making in classroom contexts. Drawing on recent empirical research, we find that LLMs demonstrate significant promise in generating SJT items with psychometric properties comparable to expert-developed assessments, while substantially reducing development time and resource costs. However, LLMs also exhibit systematic biases—including racial, gender, and socioeconomic biases—when evaluating teaching scenarios and generating educational content. These biases manifest across multiple modalities, from text-based evaluations to vision-language models processing classroom imagery. We synthesize findings on LLM capabilities in automated scenario generation, response analysis, and simulation-based training, while critically examining the ethical implications of algorithmic bias in teacher evaluation. The article concludes with recommendations for responsible integration, emphasizing the necessity of human oversight, critical digital pedagogy, and continuous bias auditing in teacher education programs.

OpenAI OpCo LLC, decided by the Delhi High Court on 24 July 2026, concerning the use of copyrighted news content for training generative artificial intelligence. It analyses the Court's approach to territorial jurisdiction, copyright infringement, AI-generated outputs, and fair dealing under Section 52(1)(a) of the Copyright Act, 1957. The comment critically evaluates the interpretation of private use, research, commercial purpose, and public interest in AI training. It highlights concerns regarding lawful data sourcing, licensing markets, and creator compensation, emphasising the need for legislative clarity to balance technological innovation with copyright protection.

items.title: Catalysts, Not Only Constraints: Pre-Service EFL Teacher Agency in Generative AI-Assisted Lesson Planning
items.abstract: This study explores how pre-service English as a foreign language (EFL) teachers used three Generative AI (GenAI) tools, ChatGPT, Gemini, and DeepSeek, while planning and teaching lessons. Drawing on ecological model of teacher agency, it examines how perceived limitations of these tools were associated with different forms of teacher agency, and whether the limitations associated with each form varied across tools. Using a qualitative case study design, the study draws on 58 participants’ reflective essays and observations of 13 classroom lessons. Findings reveal three forms of agency: recontextualizing (adapting generic AI content locally), substitutive (rejecting and replacing impractical suggestions), and improvisational (spontaneous in-class adjustments), each associated with different types of limitations. As a conceptual contribution, the study proposes a three-part typology of teacher agency based on the chordal triad model, and offers recommendations for EFL teacher education, highlighting the need for critical AI literacy and context-sensitive use of multiple GenAI tools.

items.title: Chart the Invisible: Interactive Perception for Hidden-Target Exploration in GUI Agents
items.abstract: Despite rapid progress in command-line interface (CLI) tasks, recent LLM-based agents still struggle with reliable task execution through graphical user interfaces (GUIs). A key challenge is the limited content visible within a bounded viewport, especially on mobile devices, where many task-relevant targets remain hidden and can only be revealed through swipe interactions. Therefore, although most GUI agents support swipe as an action primitive, the lack of target visibility makes it difficult for them to decide when, where, and how to swipe to reveal the hidden content. Our quantitative study further shows that GUI agents incorrectly choose a click action in 47.8% of cases that require swipe exploration. To bridge this gap, this paper proposes equipping GUI agents with scrollable-region perception to support hidden-area exploration before action selection. To this end, we trained the first multimodal model for scrollable-region perception on a manually collected dataset of 667 UI screens, called Hagasu. By correctly identifying 78.5% of scrollable regions, experiments across nine GUI agents show that integrating Hagasu improves the mean end-to-end completion rate from 64.8% to 82.7% on explore-dependent tasks. To facilitate follow-up research, we release the swipe dataset and the source code of Hagasu.

items.title: Chatbots and beyond: transforming cannabis use interventions with innovative AI approaches
items.abstract: Cannabis use and dependence is a rising public health challenge worldwide. Globally, the number of people with cannabis use disorder and its associated burden of diseases have notably increased in the past decades, particularly affecting young people [1,2]. Despite this rising burden, public health responses remain limited.While there are no established pharmacological treatments for cannabis use and dependence, psychosocial approaches, including motivational and cognitive-behavioral interventions, may improve cannabis use outcomes [3]. However, access to these treatments remains limited by workforce, time and transportation barriers. Treatment-related stigma, shaped by histories of drug control and enforcement that unevenly affect underserved populations, also discourages formal help-seeking [4]. Moreover, existing interventions are rarely delivered when people need support most and are often minimally responsive to changing risk states and individual needs. In this context, recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) create an opportunity to address these gaps by making cannabis interventions more accessible, scalable, timely, and personalized.AI conversational chatbots are one promising approach. In practice, chatbots could be engineered to deliver core elements of psychosocial interventions for cannabis use by helping users set goals, identify triggers, strengthen motivation, and practice coping and relapse-prevention skills. A recent systematic review of chatbot-assisted substance use interventions, mainly for tobacco and alcohol use, found that experimental studies reported meaningful effects on substance use outcomes and users generally found the interventions useful and acceptable [5]. Importantly, chatbots could address existing access gaps by providing private, on-demand support outside conventional clinic settings and extending services to people facing geographic, transportation, scheduling, or stigma-related barriers. They could scale up at exceptionally low marginal costs, reducing reliance on scarce trained professionals. AI could also improve the timeliness of cannabis use interventions through just-in-time adaptive interventions (JITAIs). JITAIs can use machine learning methods to identify moments of heightened vulnerability and trigger support in a timely manner, although evidence of their effectiveness for substance use remains limited [6]. For cannabis use, this could involve drawing on self-reported data, prior engagement patterns, time, location, or other digital signals to identify vulnerable moments, such as craving after work, social exposure to use, boredom at night, or stress after conflict. The intervention could then provide a real-time response, such as a motivational message, coping prompt, or brief cognitive-behavioral exercise. Because cannabis use risk is often episodic and context-dependent, JITAIs could complement psychosocial approaches by delivering their content at high-risk moments rather than only in scheduled or user-initiated sessions.Conversational chatbots and JITAIs could be combined in intervention design. In such a model, the JITAI component identifies moments of heightened risk using self-reported, behavioral, or contextual data, while the chatbot delivers support in a conversational format, which could be personalized to adapt to the user's current state. For example, a recent smoking-cessation intervention integrated JITAI with a generative chatbot and was evaluated favorably by a domain expert [7].While direct evidence remains limited, certain elements of psychosocial interventions for tobacco use may be adaptable to cannabis interventions, as these substances overlap in psychosocial processes such as motivation, cravings, triggers, coping, and relapse. This possibility is supported by evidence that cannabis co-users who reduced cigarette use in a smoking cessation intervention may concurrently reduce their cannabis use, even though cannabis use was not explicitly addressed [8]. Therefore, existing evidence on tobacco interventions [5,7] could support the feasibility of AI-enabled cannabis use interventions.Nevertheless, adaptation would be required to account for the unique characteristics of cannabis use, including diverse products and routes of administration, self-medication, associations with social identity, and legal status. Above all, innovative AI interventions for cannabis use must be designed with safety and privacy as core requirements. A review found over half of health-related chatbots failed to respond adequately to high-risk messages such as suicidal thoughts [9]. Such limitations may become particularly consequential in cannabis interventions, where users may experience psychotic symptoms or other crises. AI systems also raise privacy concerns because they may collect sensitive behavioral data, infer vulnerability, and transmit information across systems that users do not fully understand [10]. Depending on the jurisdiction, intervention data may be subject to compelled disclosure in legal or administrative proceedings. Systems should therefore have a clearly limited clinical scope, minimize data collection and retention, clearly explain any limits of confidentiality, and provide reliable escalation pathways to human support.In summary, AI approaches could substantially extend the reach of psychosocial support for cannabis use and warrant more sustained research. Design, development and evaluation of innovative AI interventions should extend beyond a focus on efficacy to considerations of whether these tools improve engagement and reduce access and stigma-related barriers without safety or privacy concerns. Future implementation research should identify which populations benefit or remain underserved, establish reliable pathways to human care, and examine how effective innovations can be integrated into routine care and public health infrastructure.

items.title: Cheap AI-Assisted Reverse Engineering and What It Will Do
items.abstract: Generative AI is putting the law of reverse engineering (RE) under severe strain. Existing IP and technology laws assume that RE is expensive and time-consuming, and that it requires specialized expertise. They generally allow it, but they rely on its difficulty as a filter to separate (permissible) RE from (impermissible) copying and theft. Generative AI is changing this equation by making \RE much faster, cheaper, and easier. AI systems can identify hardware components, extract firmware, decompile object code, and clone entire apps. The resulting struggle between technology vendors and reverse engineers will challenge a wide range of laws, including trade secret, copyright, anti-circumvention, computer misuse, and contract. In this article, we describe the ways in which AI is changing \RE, map these new practices onto existing laws, and sketch ways that the legal system could respond and their associated trade-offs.

items.title: Choosing Cardiovascular Assessment and Risk-Prediction Tools Across the Care Pathway
items.abstract: Cardiovascular diseases remain a leading cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide, making accurate and efficient risk stratification essential across the care pathway. Numerous tools support emergency triage, disease assessment, procedural decision-making, long-term prevention, atrial fibrillation management, and evaluation of functional status, but no single model is applicable across all clinical settings or populations. This clinician-oriented review categorizes and critically compares commonly used cardiovascular assessment and risk-prediction tools, including History, Electrocardiogram, Age, Risk factors, Troponin, Global Registry of Acute Coronary Events, and Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction for emergency triage; Agatston, Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis, and Synergy Between Percutaneous Coronary Intervention with Taxus and Cardiac Surgery for anatomical and clinical assessment; European System for Cardiac Operative Risk Evaluation, Society of Thoracic Surgeons, and Revised Cardiac Risk Index, for procedural risk; and Framingham, the pooled cohort equations implemented in the Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease, Risk Estimator, Systematic Coronary Risk Evaluation 2, QResearch Cardiovascular Risk Algorithm 3, and Predicting Risk of Cardiovascular Disease EVENTs for long-term prediction. Congestive heart failure, hypertension, age ≥75, diabetes, stroke/transient ischemic attack (2 points), congestive heart failure, hypertension, age ≥75 (2 points), diabetes, stroke/TIA (2 points), vascular disease, age 65-74, sex category (female), and hypertension, abnormal renal/liver function, stroke, bleeding history, labile international normalized ratio, elderly, drugs/alcohol, are discussed in the context of atrial fibrillation, alongside New York Heart Association and the Seattle Angina Questionnaire as measures of functional status and quality of life. For each tool, we examine its clinical purpose, principal variables, strengths, limitations, practical applications, and areas of overlap. Differences in implementation across healthcare systems and patient populations are considered to support context-appropriate selection. Persistent limitations include poor standardization, reliance on data that may be unavailable in resource-constrained settings, limited transportability, and incomplete integration into clinical workflows. Greater harmonization, external validation, digital automation, and the careful incorporation of biomarkers and artificial intelligence may support more accessible, dynamic, and personalized cardiovascular risk assessment.

items.title: Climate-adaptive machine learning-driven analysis of a hybrid parabolic trough collector-based cogeneration system with steam turbine, thermoelectric generator, and phase change material for environmental sustainability
items.abstract: The biggest obstacle to the widespread adoption of solar energy technologies is the impact of regional climatic conditions on production interruptions and performance degradation. This study presents a novel artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted simulation framework that analyses the techno-economic feasibility of an experimentally validated hybrid parabolic trough collector (PTC), steam turbine, thermoelectric generator (TEG), and phase change material (PCM) system across Türkiye. Within the scope of the study, high-resolution meteorological data (2005–2023) from 11 different provinces are processed, and the system’s thermal losses due to temperature and wind are modelled with dynamic correction factors. The developed k-means clustering algorithm classifies the provinces according to their investment potential, and an autonomous decision mechanism is implemented for each region, switching between 6-bar (TEG-driven) and 14-bar (turbine-driven) operating modes. Simulation results indicate that the proposed AI-based dynamic operating strategy enhances annual energy production by 22.7%, particularly in regions with low insolation potential, such as Istanbul, and transitions the system from an idle state to an economically viable state. In regions with high potential (e.g. Antalya and Van), the system’s levelised cost of energy (LCOE) is reduced to $0.04/kWh, while payback periods are mitigated to less than 3.5 years with the inclusion of carbon tax revenues under the EU Green Deal (CBAM). Residential-scale scenario analyses highlight that the hybrid system reaches the capacity to meet 100% of household demand in the summer months, selling energy to the grid, and minimising its water footprint. This study serves as a national roadmap demonstrating the applicability of hybrid solar systems not only on the southern coast but also in challenging climate zones.

items.title: Clinical Safety Thresholds and Decision Risks of Search-Augmented Large Language Models in Acute Pancreatitis: A Guideline-Anchored Evaluation for Surgical Practice
items.abstract: Background Patients and clinicians increasingly consult search-augmented Large Language Models (LLMs) for point-of-care decision support. However, their safety thresholds against newly revised guidelines remain unverified. This study established a safety baseline evaluating the clinical accuracy, completeness, quality, and readability of ChatGPT-5.3 and Gemini 3.0 Flash anchored to the 2025 IAP/APA acute pancreatitis guidelines. Methods Twenty-seven consensus-derived clinical scenarios spanning diagnosis, management, intervention, and discharge were queried using zero-shot prompts. Three blinded general surgeons evaluated outputs using 5-point Likert scales for accuracy, completeness, and Global Quality Score (GQS), alongside binary error metrics. Readability was quantified via FRES, FKGL, and SMOG indices. Inter-rater agreement was assessed using Intraclass Correlation Coefficients (ICC). Results Gemini demonstrated significantly higher completeness than ChatGPT (median [IQR]: 4.33 [4.33-4.67] vs 4.33 [4.00-4.33]; corrected P = .042); Global Quality Scores did not differ significantly (corrected P = .231). Clinical accuracy was comparable ( P = .217). Response-level hallucination rates were similar (ChatGPT: 25.9% vs Gemini: 22.2%; P = 1.000). One fatal error (advocating premature necrosectomy) occurred in the Gemini cohort (3.7%). High-score concentration induced a ceiling effect, attenuating ICC values. Both models operated at a 12th-grade reading level. ChatGPT’s quality correlated positively with word count (ρ = 0.419, P < .05), whereas Gemini maintained volume-independent density. Conclusion Both LLMs display strong baseline fidelity to the 2025 IAP/APA guidelines. However, persistent critical errors and high academic reading levels preclude autonomous deployment. Establishing this safety floor is an indispensable prerequisite for human-in-the-loop usability trials, positioning LLMs strictly as supervised clinical co-pilots.

items.title: Co-Creating Fast Fashion with AIGC: Toward New Efficiencies and Creative Practices
items.abstract: The rapid development of AI-generated content (AIGC) is profoundly impacting fast fashion design processes. While existing research has largely emphasized AIGC’s role in enhancing efficiency and expanding the design space, there remains a lack of empirical analysis grounded in real-world contexts regarding how it influences creative decision-making, iterative mechanisms, and the role of designers in actual design processes. Drawing on a human–AI collaboration perspective, this study systematically examines the impact of AIGC on fast fashion design efficiency, iterative structures, and role reconfiguration through a comparative experiment, a questionnaire survey (N = 157), and semi-structured interviews (N = 10). The study found that AIGC reduces the marginal cost of the generation and revision of design alternatives, alters the exploration and convergence mechanisms in fast fashion front-end design, and shifts the design process from a linear progression to a structured model of “parallel generation of multiple alternatives–rapid comparison–iterative convergence.” However, it also increases the pressure to filter options and gives rise to potential risks such as stylistic convergence and algorithmic dependence. The results indicate that AIGC has not replaced designers but has instead driven a shift in their roles from direct producers of visual proposals to constraint setters, outcome evaluators, and style integrators. This study provides an empirically grounded account of how AIGC is embedded in professional fast fashion design workflows, offering empirical insights into human–AI collaboration, creative decision-making, and design process governance within high-speed design systems.

items.title: Co-Design Bench: Multimodal Collaborative Coding Evaluation for Agentic Models
items.abstract: Evaluating human-AI co-design requires testing whether coding agents can translate real users' multimodal requests into working application revisions. We introduce Co-Design Bench, a reference-free benchmark of 273 tasks curated from 37,463 deduplicated queries across 26,314 real user coding sessions. Its two tracks, Multimodal Editing (ME) and Repository Editing (RE), cover localized edits with optional image, audio, video, or document inputs and coordinated repository revisions. Tasks span three capability dimensions: Grounded Understanding, UI Transformation, and Functional Implementation. The tasks pair normalized requests and runnable pre-edit applications with 2,331 hidden expert-authored acceptance criteria. Our judge-then-refute protocol grades criteria using source and browser evidence, challenges positive verdicts with a separate LLM verifier, and audits visual and interaction claims without gold code or target screenshots. Under a shared agentic harness, the strongest of ten model endpoints passes an average of 69.9% of criteria per task but fully satisfies only 26.4% of tasks. All ten endpoints achieve lower criterion completion on repository edits spanning three or four change types than on those spanning one or two. Co-Design Bench provides a testbed for studying the gap between partial requirement satisfaction and complete task success under agentic execution for real-user application revisions.

items.title: Co‐existing and co‐constructing with AI: Beliefs, practices, and professional readiness of online language coaches
items.abstract: Abstract This study examines how online Spanish language coaches, that is, trained native speakers who facilitate authentic conversational practice, perceive and use artificial intelligence (AI) in virtual language teaching. While previous research has predominantly focused on classroom teachers, we use a mixed‐methods design that includes a questionnaire and open‐ended responses from 96 coaches based in 15 Spanish‐speaking countries. We examine their familiarity with AI, attitudes toward its use, and views on how it may complement human interaction in language learning. Coaches see clear benefits in using AI for lesson planning, personalization, and idea generation, but they also express concerns about data privacy and ethics, misinformation, reduced critical thinking, and the loss of emotional connection and cultural authenticity. Regression analyses show that familiarity with AI and comfort using it are the strongest predictors of perceived usefulness and willingness to integrate this technology into practice. The findings suggest that professional development should strengthen AI literacy while preserving the interpersonal and intercultural dimensions of language learning. Clear institutional guidance is also needed on AI use and pedagogical approaches that integrate AI without diminishing meaningful human interaction.

items.title: COLLABRO AI Ecosystem: A Collaborative Multi-Agent Architecture for Conversational Assistance, Autonomous Software Engineering and Audio Intelligence
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence tools for conversation, programming and speech are usually built and used in isolation, which forces users to carry context manually from one tool to another. This paper presents the COLLABRO AI Ecosystem, a multi-agent platform that unifies conversational assistance, autonomous software engineering and audio intelligence within a single coordinated architecture. Natural Language Processing (NLP), Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) techniques are used to interpret user input, infer intent and decompose goals into tasks. An orchestrator agent routes these tasks to specialised agents for dialogue, code understanding, generation and debugging, and speech and audio analysis. A shared context store lets the agents maintain a unified understanding of the user’s goal, exchange intermediate artefacts and improve through feedback. A governance layer embeds data privacy, transparency and responsible automation into every agent interaction. We describe the architecture, the coordination and routing workflow, candidate implementation techniques and the ethical safeguards, and we propose an evaluation protocol with per-agent and cross-agent metrics. The modular design supports software development, enterprise automation, content creation and accessibility applications. This paper reports design and methodology; no quantitative performance results are claimed, and measured evaluation is identified as future work.

items.title: Comparative analysis of end-to-end learning and foundation models for clinical-grade prostate pathology
items.abstract: Abstract Foundation models (FMs) using self-supervised pre-training are widely advocated as a universal solution for pathology, yet their advantages over task-specific (TS) models remain unclear. Here we show, using over 100,000 prostate biopsies from 6268 patients across 15 sites, that while FMs demonstrate utility in data-scarce scenarios, their performance converges with—and is in some cases surpassed by—TS models with sufficient labeled training data. Concordance with pathologists’ grading reaches quadratic Cohen’s kappas of 0.91 (95% CI 0.90-0.92; all models) on internal and 0.87 (0.86-0.88; TS), 0.86 (0.84-0.87; UNI FM) and 0.85 (0.84-0.86; Virchow2 FM) on external cohorts at full training. Task-specific training markedly reduces misgrading, misdiagnosis of challenging morphologies, and technical variability. Notably, FMs consume up to 35 times more energy. We advocate for considering both FMs and end-to-end learning for robust, resource-efficient, and clinically applicable AI pathology.

items.title: Comparative Evaluation of Gesture, Voice, and Mouse Modalities Using ISO 9241-9 in Controlled and Uncontrolled Environments
items.abstract: Human-robot interaction requires intuitive, efficient, and affordable interfaces for real-world deployment. This work presents a cost-effective comparative study of three interaction modalities such as gesture, voice, and mouse using the ISO 9241-9 pointing task. Twenty participants performed repeated trials in both controlled indoor and uncontrolled outdoor environments. Movement time was analyzed using Fitts’ Law, while cognitive workload and usability were evaluated using NASA-TLX and the System Usability Score. Results show a significant effect of modality on performance, where mouse achieved the lowest movement time, gesture demonstrated comparable performance with no significant difference, and voice exhibited significantly higher delays. Subjective analysis indicates lower workload for mouse, while usability scores remain high across all modalities. Environmental conditions did not significantly affect performance. The findings highlight gesture as a low-cost and touch-less alternative suitable for human-robot interaction, particularly in accessibility-focused and real-world scenarios where conventional input devices are not feasible.

items.title: Conflicting extractive futures: Exploring sociotechnical imaginaries of lithium mining in Portugal
items.abstract: Plans for lithium mining in Northern Portugal are an ongoing controversy, thematizing conflicting understandings of sociotechnical futures and generating significant local opposition and sociopolitical and academic debate. This paper draws on the framework of Sociotechnical Imaginaries (STI) to examine the distinct co-productions of natural, social and epistemological orders informing this controversy. The paper is supported by a qualitative methodology, drawing on 40 semi-structured interviews conducted between 2020-2022 with a wide range of stakeholders: State representatives, local politicians, members of parliament, local residents, representatives of anti-mining movements and environmental and climate organizations, stakeholders from mining companies and academics. The article identifies three main STI of li-mining in Portugal: Imaginary 1 – Development; Imaginary 2 – Risks; Imaginary 3 – Counterhegemony. To make sense of these conflicting extractive futures, the paper advances a conceptual framework based on three main dimensions - Place, Publics and Economics – arguing that different versions of nature, society and knowledge are enacted throughout these heterogenous STI. The main academic contribution of this article is the development of a conceptual framework to analyze conflicting STI of extractive futures, engaging with scholarship on alternative, contested and bounded imaginaries. Additionally, the article contributes to social science scholarship on lithium mining in Portugal, developing a nuanced understanding of the socio-material and epistemological dimensions underpinning this conflict.

items.title: Contextual AI Coding Assistants in Professional Practice: A Mixed-Methods Investigation of Perceptions, Benefits, and Experience-Based Challenges
items.abstract: The integration of contextual AI coding assistants, such as GitHub Copilot and ChatGPT, promises productivity gains, yet their adoption depends on complex human factors. This mixed-methods study examines how professional developers perceive, adopt, and integrate these tools, with a focus on experience-related differences. Guided by UTAUT2 and trustin-automation theory, we surveyed 219 developers across four experience tiers and interviewed 14 practitioners. Adoption intentions were associated less with perceived ease of use than with trust calibration centered on output quality. Active verification and strategic integration were positively associated with technical friction, suggesting an exposure effect. Although core perceptions were similar across experience levels, mid-career developers reported stronger performance motivation and friction sensitivity, while senior developers used more refined friction-management strategies. We propose the Trust-Calibration Adoption Framework, extending UTAUT2 by positioning output trustworthiness and experiential learning as central mechanisms. The exploratory findings require replication.

items.title: CRIM: Composable and Reusable Item Memory for Efficient Personalized Retrieval
items.abstract: Large language models incur substantial training and inference costs in personalized search and recommendation, as growing interaction histories lengthen request inputs and repeatedly expose the same item text to the model. We propose \textbf{C}omposable and \textbf{R}eusable \textbf{I}tem \textbf{M}emory (CRIM), a framework that separates item-level semantic encoding from request-level history modeling. A small set of learnable summary tokens compresses each item into compact continuous memories, while segment-level readout tokens (REC tokens) introduce predictive supervision within the interaction history. These memories are independent of users and queries and can therefore be reused across requests. At inference time, CRIM composes cached memories in interaction order and incorporates an optional query to produce a personalized retrieval representation, reducing repeated item-text encoding while retaining request-dependent contextual modeling. We further introduce a joint training mechanism that combines cached memories with sampled live re-encoding. Re-encoding only a few history items per request allows the retrieval objective to jointly optimize the item and request encoders at limited computational cost, while periodic cache refreshes maintain consistency. Extensive evaluation and cost analysis on MovieLens-1M, Qilin, and our new LazSeq dataset show that CRIM achieves state-of-the-art retrieval performance with substantially lower inference costs at the same backbone scale, while limiting item re-encoding during joint training. We will publicly release our code and dataset.

items.title: Cross-level pathways from teacher autonomy support to adolescent intrinsic motivation through basic psychological need satisfaction: a multilevel mediation model with classroom climate as a boundary condition
items.abstract: Introduction Teacher autonomy support is associated with adolescent intrinsic motivation, but the shared classroom context is often omitted from analyses. Drawing on self-determination theory and achievement goal theory, this study examined indirect associations through autonomy, competence and relatedness need satisfaction and their moderation by classroom motivational climate. Methods Cross-sectional questionnaire data were collected from 2,634 students in 72 secondary-school classes across grades 7–12. A two-level structural equation model with random slopes separated within-class and between-class pathways. Measurement invariance was evaluated across three grade bands. Indirect effects and pairwise contrasts were assessed using 20,000 Monte Carlo draws, and mastery and performance climates were tested as cross-level moderators. Results Scalar measurement invariance supported pooling the grade bands. All three indirect effects were positive at both levels. Within-class estimates through autonomy, competence and relatedness were 0.148, 0.102 and 0.068, respectively; between-class estimates were 0.256, 0.167 and 0.154. Explained variance in intrinsic motivation was 31% within classes and 47% between classes. Pairwise contrasts favored autonomy over the other needs, with weaker evidence for its advantage over competence; competence and relatedness were not statistically distinguishable. The between-class joint equality test was borderline. Mastery climate strengthened the first-stage autonomy and competence paths, whereas performance climate weakened them. Neither moderator was significant for the relatedness path. Discussion The findings support distinguishing individual perceptions from shared classroom conditions when studying autonomy-supportive teaching. Classroom climate may help explain variation in the associations between perceived support, need satisfaction and intrinsic motivation. Because the study was cross-sectional and relied on student self-report, the estimated indirect pathways do not establish causal or temporal ordering.

items.title: Cultivating high-reliable organizing: A holistic perspective
items.abstract: High-reliable organizing (HRO) has long been associated with how organizations sustain reliable performance under conditions of complexity, uncertainty, and change. While Mindful Organizing (MO), and Resilience Engineering (RE) have generated important theoretical insights, guidance on how organizations can cultivate HRO in everyday organizing remains fragmented. This conceptual essay develops a holistic perspective that positions HRO as an ongoing accomplishment rather than a fixed organizational capability or the outcome of implementing isolated concepts. Through a systematic comparison of the five established MO processes and the four resilience potentials, we show how the two perspectives can be related while preserving their distinct analytical orientations. MO focuses on the collective organizing through which people notice, interpret, coordinate, and respond to emerging situations, while RE emphasizes organizational potentials to monitor, respond, anticipate, and learn under changing conditions. Building on this synthesis, we develop the holistic framework of HRO, identify two additional organizing processes— preoccupation with things that go right and self-awareness —and develop an approach to cultivating and operationalizing HRO through collaborative inquiry, driving forces, and situated practices. Rather than prescribing predefined practices, we argue that organizations can cultivate mindsets and directions of attention that guide how established concepts are translated to context-sensitive action while remaining grounded in the scientific foundations of HRO, MO, and RE. The essay contributes a theoretically grounded perspective for understanding and cultivating high-reliable organizing as an ongoing accomplishment in complex sociotechnical systems.
